summary: Deep web research on SOTA techniques to lift MFU/TPW/MBU, assessed for what a CUDA-interposition substrate can actually deliver, synthesized into a product direction

research.summary: Speculative decoding is the canonical way to spend the ~95% idle decode-time compute: draft K tokens cheaply, verify them in ONE target forward pass, accept the longest correct prefix — exact-output-preserving with greedy/tree verification. The 2023-2026 SOTA splits into trained-head methods (EAGLE-3 / EAGLE-3.1, Medusa, DeepSeek-MTP: highest acceptance, ~2-2.5x single-user, but need a trained draft head/MTP module bolted onto the target) and draft-free methods (ngram/prompt-lookup, lookahead, SuffixDecoding: no model artifact, 2-5.3x on input-grounded/agentic workloads, near-0 on free-form text). The decisive serving fact, measured repeatedly (vLLM, Red Hat, "Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right"): the gain is a LOW-QPS / SMALL-BATCH / memory-bound phenomenon — once the server is compute-bound (high concurrency, large batch), wasted verification FLOPs on rejected tokens turn speculation NEGATIVE (up to 1.4-1.8x SLOWDOWN, -30% throughput). MagicDec is the one regime where spec-decode helps at large batch, but only for long-context where KV-cache (not weights) is the bottleneck. CRITICAL for CIPHER: every one of these methods lives in the serving runtime's scheduler/sampler/attention path (build a draft tree, append speculative tokens to the sequence, run tree/causal-mask verification, run acceptance sampling) — this is ABOVE the GEMM/kernel layer. A pure CUDA-driver-interposition substrate that GOT-patches cuBLAS cannot construct candidates, mutate the token sequence, or run verification; it would need vLLM integration (framework change) or, for trained-head methods, a model-side artifact too.

techniques.name: EAGLE-3 / EAGLE-3.1 (trained feature-level draft head)
techniques.mechanism: A lightweight single-layer transformer draft head consumes the target model's fused multi-layer feature vectors (not token embeddings) to autoregressively draft a token TREE, verified in one target forward pass with tree attention; EAGLE-3.1 lengthens accepted length further and adds parallel drafting.
techniques.reported_gain: vLLM/Red Hat: up to 1.8x lower latency on Llama-3.1-8B and ~1.6x on Llama-3.3-70B at LOW request rate (avg accepted length ~1.74-2.2 tokens), 'up to 2.5x' overall; EAGLE-3.1 on Kimi-K2.6-NVFP4 (vLLM, GB200): 2.03x per-user output throughput at concurrency 1, decaying to 1.71x@C=4 and 1.66x@C=16; degrades/goes negative when compute-bound at high QPS. EAGLE-3 beats Medusa-2 by ~15-25% tok/s at batch 1-4 (Spheron/SpecForge).
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode), by converting spare compute into tokens/weight-stream; only in memory-bound regime
techniques.model_dependency: trained draft head per target model (EAGLE-3 head trained on target's hidden features); tree-verification must run inside the serving runtime
techniques.impl_cost: head training: days-weeks per model on a framework like SpecForge; serving integration: already in vLLM. Substrate cannot host either.

techniques.name: Medusa / Medusa-2 (parallel trained decoding heads)
techniques.mechanism: Bolt N extra MLP heads onto the frozen target's last hidden state; head k predicts the token at offset k independently; candidates assembled into a tree and verified in one pass. Simpler than EAGLE but heads don't share context so acceptance falls off faster at longer speculation.
techniques.reported_gain: Medusa paper reports ~2.2-2.8x wall-clock on Vicuna/Zephyr single-user; consistently BEATEN by EAGLE-3 (EAGLE-3 ~15-25% higher tok/s at batch 1-4 on H100). Acceptance drops faster than EAGLE at long-form generation.
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode), memory-bound regime only
techniques.model_dependency: trained Medusa heads per target model; tree verification in serving runtime
techniques.impl_cost: head training days; verification integration is framework-level. Substrate cannot deliver.

techniques.name: DeepSeek-style Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) module
techniques.mechanism: An auxiliary transformer module trained jointly with the base model predicts multiple future tokens from the same hidden state; at inference it acts as a self-contained drafter whose tokens are verified in parallel (self-speculation).
techniques.reported_gain: DeepSeek-V3 tech report: 2nd-token acceptance 85-90%, ~1.8x TPS; SGLang/practical serving reports 1.2-2.1x latency+throughput. Requires the MTP module to be trained INTO the model (DeepSeek-V3 added ~14B params for it).
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode)
techniques.model_dependency: MTP head trained jointly with the base model (architectural); not retrofittable to an arbitrary Mistral/Llama-7B checkpoint without training
techniques.impl_cost: must be part of pretraining/finetuning; not a deployment-time lever. Substrate cannot deliver.

techniques.name: Prompt-Lookup / N-gram Decoding (DRAFT-FREE)
techniques.mechanism: No model: match the most-recent generated n-gram against the prompt (and prior output) via string lookup, propose the following tokens as the draft, verify in one target pass. Zero training, zero extra weights.
techniques.reported_gain: vLLM/Red Hat: up to 2.8x at QPS=1 on Llama-3-70B CNN/DailyMail summarization (4xH100); large on input-grounded tasks (summarization, RAG, code-edit, QA) where output copies the input, ~0 on free-form generation. HIGH-QPS: 1.8x SLOWDOWN measured.
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode), low-QPS only; task-dependent
techniques.model_dependency: none (no draft model, no heads) — but candidate construction + tree/sequence append + verification all run in the serving runtime
techniques.impl_cost: already in vLLM as speculative_model='[ngram]'; building it as a CUDA-interposition substrate is not feasible (needs token-sequence + sampler access). Days IF done as a vLLM plugin, not as substrate.

techniques.name: SuffixDecoding (DRAFT-FREE, suffix-tree, best model-free serving result)
techniques.mechanism: Build a suffix tree over current-request tokens + a GLOBAL tree over prior outputs; expand the highest-empirical-probability continuation into a speculation tree; verify in one pass. Model-free, exact-output-preserving. Targets agentic/repetitive workloads.
techniques.reported_gain: NeurIPS-2025 spotlight: up to 5.3x vs vanilla on AgenticSQL (per-task peaks 9-10x), 2.5x mean on SWE-Bench; 2.8x faster than EAGLE-2/3, 1.9x faster than Token Recycling, 1.3-3x over Prompt-Lookup. Measured ONLINE in vLLM at concurrency 8 / 4xH100 TP=4, end-to-end 1.8-4.5x on SWE-Bench, output distribution preserved (37.2% task completion matched).
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode); shines on agentic/repetitive serving where prior outputs recur
techniques.model_dependency: none (no draft model / no heads); needs a cross-request suffix-tree store + candidate injection + tree verification inside the runtime
techniques.impl_cost: weeks as a vLLM-integrated component (suffix-tree store + tree-attention verify). NOT a GEMM-interposition deliverable — needs token-sequence + scheduler access.

techniques.name: Lookahead Decoding (DRAFT-FREE, Jacobi n-gram)
techniques.mechanism: Run Jacobi fixed-point iteration to generate+cache n-grams from the model's own parallel forward passes, then verify them — no draft model, no datastore. Trades extra FLOPs/step for fewer sequential steps.
techniques.reported_gain: LMSYS: ~1.5-2.3x latency reduction single-user (e.g. ~1.8x on MT-Bench, ~2x+ on code) by reducing decode steps; gains are FLOP-for-latency trades that vanish/reverse once compute-bound (high batch). Not a throughput win under load.
techniques.axis: latency (decode steps), single-user / low-batch only; consumes compute so it hurts at high batch
techniques.model_dependency: none; but needs custom attention masks (parallel n-gram verification) and sequence manipulation in the runtime
techniques.impl_cost: framework-level (custom mask/kernel + sequence logic). Not substrate-deliverable.

techniques.name: Self-speculative / LayerSkip (early-exit draft from same weights)
techniques.mechanism: Use the target model's own EARLY layers (with trained early-exit) to draft, later layers to verify — one model, no separate draft weights. Needs LayerSkip-style training (layer dropout + early-exit loss) for good acceptance.
techniques.reported_gain: LayerSkip paper / HF: up to ~2.0x speedup with high acceptance when the model is LayerSkip-trained; on an off-the-shelf model without that training, acceptance is poor.
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode), low-batch regime
techniques.model_dependency: early-exit-trained model (LayerSkip) for good acceptance; plus runtime support to run a partial forward as the drafter
techniques.impl_cost: training to enable; runtime change to do partial-depth drafting. Substrate cannot deliver.

techniques.name: Draft-model speculative decoding (separate small model)
techniques.mechanism: A small standalone model (e.g. 0.5B-1B) drafts K tokens, the large target verifies in one pass. Classic Leviathan/Chen speculative sampling; exact-output-preserving.
techniques.reported_gain: vLLM: 1.5x at QPS=1 on Llama-3-70B/ShareGPT with a 0.5B drafter (4xH100); explicitly 1.4x SLOWDOWN at high QPS. The original lever but lowest-acceptance vs EAGLE; needs a quality-matched draft model.
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (decode), low-QPS only — negative at high QPS
techniques.model_dependency: a separate small draft model that shares the target's tokenizer/distribution (a model artifact); verification + acceptance sampling in the runtime
techniques.impl_cost: the draft model must exist; orchestration is vLLM-native. Substrate cannot run a second model's forward pass or the acceptance logic.

techniques.name: MagicDec (spec-decode that WINS at large batch / long context)
techniques.mechanism: Identifies that at large batch + long context the bottleneck is KV-cache loading, not weights; uses a self-speculation drafter with a FIXED small KV window (StreamingLLM sink) so draft cost stays flat as batch grows, restoring speedup in the high-throughput regime.
techniques.reported_gain: ICLR-2025: speedup INCREASES with batch size for moderate-to-long sequences (the opposite of normal spec-decode), e.g. up to ~2x throughput at large batch on long context (LLaMA-2/3 8B-70B); near-zero benefit at short context.
techniques.axis: throughput (decode) at LARGE batch + long context — the one regime where speculation survives compute-saturation, because there it's KV-bound not compute-bound
techniques.model_dependency: none new (self-speculation), but needs sparse-KV draft path + verification inside the runtime
techniques.impl_cost: framework-level KV-window draft + verify. Not substrate-deliverable.

techniques.name: Batch-aware / goodput-optimized scheduling of speculation (SmartSpec, EXSpec, dynamic spec length)
techniques.mechanism: Make speculation a SCHEDULER decision: pick draft length (or turn spec off) per step based on current batch size / load to maximize goodput, and fix the 'ragged tensor' correctness bug when batched sequences accept different lengths.
techniques.reported_gain: 'Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right' (EXSpec): up to 3x throughput at batch 8 over batch-1 while restoring output equivalence; degrades beyond batch 8 (alignment overhead grows ~13%@b1 to ~40%@b8/b32). SmartSpec/goodput work shows dynamic spec-length avoids the high-load slowdown that static spec-decode suffers (up to -30% at high load).
techniques.axis: throughput (serving goodput) — the control layer that decides WHEN speculation pays off
techniques.model_dependency: none extra; but the control sits in the runtime scheduler/sampler with full batch + accept-length state
techniques.impl_cost: this is the part closest to CIPHER's 'classifier/orchestrator' spirit, BUT it must read batch/accept-length state and steer the sampler — that state lives in vLLM, not at the GEMM interposition layer. A substrate could only ADVISE; the actuation needs framework hooks.
sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2406.14066v2 (Optimizing Speculative Decoding Using Goodput / SmartSpec)

assessment.technique: EAGLE-3 / EAGLE-3.1 (trained feature-level draft head + tree-verification speculative decoding)
assessment.honest_gain: The technique is real and the gains are genuine at LOW load, but they are NOT deliverable by this substrate (see substrate_reality) and they shrink hard in this team's target regime. Honest numbers for H100 / 7B-dense / vLLM / FP8, batched-saturated serving: low-load single-user latency is genuinely ~1.5-1.8x faster (Red Hat measured up to 1.8x on Llama-3.1-8B, but on A100, not H100, at low request rate). As concurrency rises the speedup decays monotonically: EAGLE-3.1 on Kimi-K2 NVFP4 (GB200) goes 2.03x@C=1 -> 1.71x@C=4 -> 1.66x@C=16 — and Kimi-K2 is a huge MoE that hides verify cost far better than a 7B dense model does. For a 7B DENSE model the decay is steeper: independent SGLang reports show EAGLE-3 falling to ~1.38x at batch=64 and ~1.13x at batch=16, and multiple serving studies report speculative decoding going NEGATIVE at high QPS (up to -30.25% vs plain autoregressive) once verification is compute-bound. That compute-bound regime is exactly this team's established 'MFU ~68%, batch>~16' operating point. So the honest expected gain for a SATURATED FP8 7B vLLM deployment is roughly break-even to mildly negative; the real win exists only in the low-concurrency / latency-SLA tail (interactive single-user), where ~1.4-1.8x p50/p99 latency is achievable — but the substrate cannot capture even that without a vLLM fork.
assessment.substrate_reality: DECISIVE BLOCKER: EAGLE-3 needs two things a GOT-patch/cuBLAS-interposition substrate cannot provide intercept-only. (1) A PER-TARGET TRAINED DRAFT HEAD: a fine-tuned checkpoint (FC layers + one decoder layer + LM head, ~850MB for the 8B) trained on the target model's fused low/mid/high hidden states (yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B etc.). Off-the-shelf heads exist for popular Llamas, so 'no retrain' is half-true for those exact models — but the head is still a NEW model that must be loaded and RUN as an autoregressive generator, which is a model/framework addition, not a kernel interception. (2) TREE-ATTENTION DRAFTING + VERIFICATION INSIDE THE RUNTIME: vLLM docs/source confirm tree attention, branch-masked single-pass verification, the eagle3 method flag, ragged/variable-accept KV-cache handling, and a custom sampler are 'core runtime requirements built directly into vLLM's speculative decoding implementation rather than plugin-based.' Capturing the target's intermediate hidden features, running the draft loop, building the tree, masking attention, managing ragged KV cache, and rewinding the sampler all live in vLLM's scheduler/model-runner — above the cuBLAS/CUDA-driver boundary the substrate patches. Intercepting GEMM calls gives the substrate no place to inject an autoregressive control loop or alter the token sampling path. Therefore intercept-only is INSUFFICIENT: delivering this requires either forking vLLM source or using vLLM's native speculative-config (which is the framework already doing it, not the substrate). The CLAIMED DELIVERABILITY 'no-needs-model-training' is misleading for this substrate: it conflates 'pretrained heads exist' with 'the substrate can host it' — the substrate cannot, regardless of whether the head is pretrained.
assessment.reasoning: Gain provenance and cherry-pick check: Red Hat Developer (2025-07-01) measured up to 1.8x (Llama-3.1-8B, single A100) and 1.6x (Llama-3.3-70B, 4xA100) at LOW request rate on MT-Bench, and explicitly warns 'at higher throughputs or batch sizes we are compute-bound and speculative decoding can provide worse performance' (https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/07/01/fly-eagle3-fly-faster-inference-vllm-speculative-decoding). The 4.1-6.5x paper headline is temp=0, batch-1, single-sequence on academic benchmarks with accepted length up to 7.5 (EAGLE-3 arXiv 2503.01840) — a best-case, not production. Independent reproductions show the collapse: SGLang EAGLE-3 ~1.38x at batch=64 and ~1.13x at batch=16. EAGLE-3.1 vLLM blog (https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-26-eagle-3-1) gives 2.03x@C=1 -> 1.71x@C=4 -> 1.66x@C=16 on Kimi-K2.6-NVFP4 (TP=4, GB200, SPEED-Bench) — a giant MoE on Blackwell, not 7B dense on H100. Production-serving critique (negative speedup, up to -30.25% at high QPS; break-even acceptance rises with batch; ragged-KV batching pain): corroborated across Optimizing Speculative Decoding via Goodput (arXiv 2406.14066), 'Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right' (arXiv 2510.22876), Nightjar (arXiv 2512.22420), and ECHO (arXiv 2604.09603). Deliverability: vLLM docs/source confirm tree attention and verification are core runtime features, draft head needs draft_tensor_parallel_size=1, eagle3 method flag (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/speculative_decoding/); HF checkpoints yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B confirm the head is a trained ~850MB model consuming fused hidden states. Net: real technique, real low-load latency win, but it lives entirely inside the serving runtime and is therefore out of reach for an intercept-only substrate without a vLLM fork; and its gain is near zero-to-negative in this team's compute-bound saturated FP8 batch regime.

assessment.technique: Medusa / Medusa-2 (parallel trained decoding heads for speculative decoding)
assessment.honest_gain: Single-user / batch-1 only. Original paper: Medusa-1 >2.2x, Medusa-2 2.3-3.6x wall-clock on Vicuna/Zephyr at batch 1, greedy/low-load (arxiv 2401.10774). NVIDIA measured up to 1.9x on Llama-3.1 (HGX H200) — already lower than paper headline, and on a fatter interconnect than a single H100. Medusa is consistently BEATEN by EAGLE-3 (~15-25% higher tok/s at batch 1-4 on H100; SGLang H100 EAGLE-3 1.81x@batch2 falling to 1.38x@batch64). For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8, PRODUCTION batched serving) the honest expected gain is ~0x to negative. Three independent sources: (1) SqueezeBits/vLLM-vs-TRT-LLM — spec decode underperforms standard decoding at high concurrency due to verification batch-expansion; recommend speculative_disable_by_batch_size; reversal around batch 32-64. (2) vLLM itself DEPRECATED speculative decoding in its v1 engine because it underperformed the non-speculative baseline at higher batch sizes. (3) "Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" (arxiv 2510.22876): ragged-tensor realignment overhead grows from 13%@batch1 to 40%@batch32, superlinear; their best fix (EXSpec) gets 3x at batch 8 vs batch 1 BUT degrades beyond batch 8 and that 3x is spec-vs-batch1, NOT vs an optimized saturated batched baseline; SGLang+EAGLE showed negative speedups across batch sizes. A saturated vLLM server (the team's own constraint: compute-bound at moderate batch, ~68% MFU ceiling) is exactly the regime where Medusa's ~290x spare-FLOP argument collapses — the spare FLOPs are consumed by other concurrent requests, so verification competes for compute instead of being free. Net: do NOT expect the paper's 2.2-3.6x; expect roughly break-even-to-loss under saturation, and even at low load EAGLE-3 dominates Medusa.
assessment.substrate_reality: The substrate (intercept-only, no model retrain, no vLLM fork) CANNOT deliver Medusa, for two independent fatal reasons. (1) MODEL TRAINING IS MANDATORY. The task input's "CLAIMED DELIVERABILITY: no-needs-model-training" is false on its face — Medusa's defining mechanism IS trained heads. The backbone is frozen, but the N extra MLP heads themselves must be trained/distilled per target model (Medusa-1 = heads on frozen backbone; Medusa-2 = heads + backbone co-trained with a special recipe; self-distillation pipeline needed when no SFT data, often LoRA). There is no GOT-patch / kernel-interception path that conjures trained head weights. The substrate intercepts cuBLAS/CUDA — it cannot fabricate new model parameters. (2) RUNTIME LIVES INSIDE THE FRAMEWORK. Tree-attention candidate assembly, the typical-acceptance verification pass, and (critically) the ragged-tensor KV-cache/position-id/attention-mask realignment all live in the vLLM model runner + scheduler. vLLM V1 supports Medusa natively via speculative_config (method medusa) precisely BECAUSE it required deep model-runner integration — it is not something an external interposer bolts on. A GEMM/kernel interceptor sees post-hoc CUDA calls; it has no hook to inject new draft heads into the forward graph, restructure the attention mask into a tree, or manage divergent per-sequence accept counts in the paged KV cache. So even granting trained heads, delivery requires model-cooperation (the trained heads) AND framework-change (runtime tree-verify + ragged handling) — both explicitly OUT of the substrate's definition. Intercept-only is nowhere close to sufficient.
assessment.reasoning: Sources: Medusa paper arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774 (Medusa-1 >2.2x, Medusa-2 2.3-3.6x, frozen backbone but TRAINED heads, self-distillation/LoRA recipe). NVIDIA Technical Blog "Low Latency Inference Chapter 1" (up to 1.9x Llama-3.1 with Medusa on HGX H200 — note the fat-interconnect, multi-GPU context, lower than paper). EAGLE-3 comparisons: Spheron/E2E/Wentao summaries and SGLang H100 production numbers (EAGLE-3 beats Medusa-2 by 15-25% tok/s at batch 1-4; 1.81x@batch2 -> 1.38x@batch64). Production-batched critiques — the load-bearing adversarial evidence: SqueezeBits blog "vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM #11 Speculative Decoding" (spec decode underperforms at high concurrency, verification batch-expansion overhead, speculative_disable_by_batch_size, reversal ~batch 32-64; TRT-LLM only helps at batch=1). Convergent conclusion: real but single-user; collapses under saturation; and undeliverable by an intercept-only substrate because it needs both trained per-model heads (model training) and in-runtime tree-verify + ragged-KV handling (framework change). EAGLE-class is strictly better where spec decode helps at all, and neither is substrate-deliverable.

assessment.technique: DeepSeek-style Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) module / self-speculative decoding
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS setup (H100, 7B dense Mistral/Llama, unmodified vLLM, FP8, production batched serving) the headline 1.8x / 85-90% acceptance does NOT transfer. (1) It is DeepSeek-V3-specific (671B MoE with a jointly-trained ~14B MTP head) and a batch-1 number. LMSYS's own MTP serving blog measures +59.8 to +60.8% throughput at 2 concurrent requests but only +14.2% at 128 concurrent on H200 — the gain collapses with load. (2) For a 7B DENSE model the retrofittable analog is an EAGLE3 draft head, not MTP. EAGLE3 papers claim 4.1-6.5x at temp=0 on academic benchmarks (single-user), but realistic off-the-shelf draft acceptance is ~40% of proposed tokens (~2.4 accepted/step), giving ~2-3x ONLY at low QPS. (3) In saturated batched serving the gain shrinks toward 1x and can go negative: vLLM deprecated spec-decode in its v1 engine at high batch; arXiv 2510.22876 reports SGLang+EAGLE negative speedups across all batch sizes and a batch-8 practical ceiling, with ragged-tensor sync eating up to 40% of compute. The newest data point (vLLM EAGLE 3.1, May 2026) is better — 2.03x at C=1, 1.66x at C=16, persists to 200 concurrent — but measured on 120B MoE models (Kimi K2.6, gpt-oss-120B), NOT 7B dense, and the curve still decays with concurrency. HONEST 7B-dense/vLLM/saturated estimate: roughly 1.1-1.4x throughput IF you train and integrate a draft head and run at modest concurrency; near break-even at full saturation. None of it is deliverable by the substrate as defined.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only is NOT sufficient — unreachable for the substrate on TWO independent grounds the no-needs-model-training claim glossed. GROUND 1 (training): True MTP is architectural, trained jointly into the base model (DeepSeek added ~14B params); not retrofittable to an arbitrary Mistral/Llama-7B checkpoint. The only retrofit path is to TRAIN an EAGLE3 draft head per target model (~1.5 H100-hours for a small model, ~277MB head; pre-trained heads exist for Llama-3.1-8B and an experimental Mistral-7B EAGLE head). That is training the substrate by definition does not do. So the literal claim no-needs-model-training is false — every usable 7B-dense variant requires training a head. GROUND 2 (framework): Even with a trained head, drafting+parallel verification is implemented at the vLLM FRAMEWORK level — config-driven --speculative-config, a custom rejection sampler, ragged KV-cache management, position-ID/attention-mask synchronization, and scheduler changes. These live in vLLM's Python decode loop, not in the cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM or CUDA-kernel calls the substrate GOT-patches. A driver-interposition layer running UNDER unmodified vLLM cannot insert a draft-then-verify-N-tokens loop, cannot rewrite the KV-cache layout, and cannot replace the sampler — doing so requires forking/modifying vLLM, which the substrate explicitly does not do. To build this the substrate would have to become a serving runtime (own the decode loop + KV cache + sampler) AND a training pipeline (the draft head) — i.e., stop being an interposition substrate. Verdict: not deliverable pure-substrate, and not deliverable even with-model-cooperation under the no-vLLM-fork constraint.

assessment.technique: Self-speculative / LayerSkip (early-exit draft from the same weights)
assessment.honest_gain:
For THIS team's setup (H100, Mistral/Llama-7B dense, vLLM, FP8, production/batched serving) the honest expected gain is ~0, and plausibly NEGATIVE on throughput. Reasons stack:
(1) LayerSkip's headline numbers are batch-1, single-user, A100 latency wins on LayerSkip-TRAINED checkpoints. The HF blog (single 80GB A100, batch appears to be 1) reports per-model "efficiency": Llama2-7B only 1.297x, Code-Llama-7B in that range, Llama3-8B 1.83x, Llama2-13B 1.746x, Llama2-70B 2.06x, Llama3.2-1B 1.80x. The "~2.0x" headline is the 70B/large-model figure; the 7B-dense number is ~1.3x, and only on the special checkpoint.
(2) On an OFF-THE-SHELF (non-LayerSkip) 7B such as stock Mistral-7B, the HF blog states early-exit self-speculative decoding is SLOWER than plain autoregressive ("intermediate-layer logits cannot be unembedded unless the model is specifically trained for that; you only get speedups for a checkpoint trained that way"). So with no retrain: negative.
(3) Even WITH a LayerSkip checkpoint, the ~1.3x is a batch-1 / low-concurrency number. Production critiques put the speculative-decoding crossover at ~4-8 concurrent requests; above ~32 the GPU is compute-bound and verification overhead eats the gain (per-request latency can rise even if token-throughput nominally holds). vLLM's own "up to 2.8x" is explicitly a low-QPS figure that decays toward 1x as load rises. A saturated FP8 vLLM fleet is exactly the regime where self-spec gives little-to-nothing. MagicDec recovers high-batch speedup ONLY for long context (KV-cache-bound, beyond a critical sequence length) — not generic short-context 7B serving.
Net for this team: do not expect a usable lift; budget 0x and treat any deployment as latency-only for batch-1 interactive traffic on a separately-trained checkpoint.
assessment.substrate_reality:
A CUDA-driver-interposition substrate (GOT-patch cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM + kernel intercept, classifier, clocks/power, runs UNDER unmodified vLLM, no retrain, no vLLM fork) CANNOT deliver this, on two independent walls:
WALL A - the control loop lives in the framework, not below it. vLLM implements self/speculative decoding entirely at engine level: the SCHEDULER allocates multiple token slots per forward pass and does per-sequence dynamic speculative length; the MEMORY MANAGER manages KV cache for BOTH the draft (early-layers) and target (full) passes; and a spec_decode_worker coordinates draft -> verify -> rejection-sampling each step. None of that is expressible by intercepting GEMM/kernel calls — the substrate sees individual GEMMs, not token slots, not KV-cache bookkeeping, not a verify/accept/rollback loop, and cannot author a partial-then-full forward with rollback of rejected tokens. Doing it intercept-only would require re-implementing vLLM's spec-decode engine below the framework, which contradicts "runs under unmodified vLLM, no fork." This is the same class of wall the team already measured in cipher-ra-path1-build-wall (vLLM owns/re-processes its own graph; external structural mutation is rejected).
WALL B - the model dependency is a hard retrain, not cooperation. Good acceptance REQUIRES LayerSkip-style continual pretraining (layer-dropout + early-exit loss so intermediate-layer hidden states are unembeddable). The substrate cannot synthesize that; off-the-shelf Mistral/Llama-7B yields net-negative self-spec. Available checkpoints (facebook/layerskip-llama2-7B, layerskip-codellama-7B, layerskip-llama3.2-1B) are SEPARATE trained models — and notably there is NO LayerSkip Mistral-7B and no LayerSkip FP8 path published; the team would have to train one, which is explicitly out of scope ("does NOT retrain models").
The most the substrate could honestly do is route/throttle: detect a self-spec-capable workload and set clocks — i.e., the DVFS lever the team already has, which is orthogonal to and does not create the speculative speedup.
assessment.reasoning:
Sources and what each establishes:
- LayerSkip paper (arXiv 2404.16710, Meta/FAIR) and HF blog "Faster Text Generation with Self-Speculative Decoding" (huggingface.co/blog/layerskip): headline acceptance E=18: 98.9%, up to 2.0x speedup; but per-model efficiency on single 80GB A100 is Llama2-7B 1.297x, Llama2-13B 1.746x, Llama2-70B 2.06x, Llama3-8B 1.83x, Llama3.2-1B 1.80x. The blog EXPLICITLY states off-the-shelf checkpoints get NO speedup ("logits from intermediate layers cannot be unembedded unless the model is specifically trained for that; you will only obtain speedups for a checkpoint trained in such a way" and baseline checkpoints are "slower than autoregressive"). Establishes: 7B gain is ~1.3x not 2x, and is conditional on a special trained checkpoint => CLAIMED "no-needs-model-training" is FALSE; it is needs-model-training.
- HF model cards facebook/layerskip-llama2-7B / -codellama-7B / -llama3.2-1B: confirms checkpoints exist only for specific Llama/CodeLlama models (no Mistral-7B, no FP8), each a continually-pretrained separate model. The card/blog note a last-layer accuracy drop on some models from the LayerSkip continual pretraining => a quality cost, not free.
- Production critique "Speculative Decoding in Production: Free Tokens and Hidden Traps" (tianpan.co, 2026-04): speculative decoding helps wall-clock latency only below ~4-8 concurrent requests; at 32+ the GPU is compute-bound and verification overhead consumes gains, per-request latency can INCREASE; viability is governed by acceptance alpha (alpha=0.6 ~2.4x, alpha=0.8 ~3.7x, below 0.5 net loss), and it names LayerSkip/Speculative-Streaming as self-spec that "sacrifice some speedup vs purpose-trained drafts," designed for interactive low-concurrency NOT throughput-optimized serving. Establishes: does NOT hold in batched/saturated production.
- General SD-at-scale results (Nightjar arXiv 2512.22420; SPEED-Bench; Doubleword Ep.13): as batch grows, system becomes compute-bound and speculative gains diminish/disappear; low acceptance wastes GPU compute. Corroborates the batch wall.
- MagicDec (arXiv 2408.11049, Together AI blog): the one regime where SD helps at high batch is LONG CONTEXT (KV-cache-bound, beyond a critical sequence length) via a fixed-window draft — NOT generic short-context 7B serving. Establishes the counter-example does not rescue this team's setup.
- vLLM spec-decode docs/blog (vllm.ai 2024-10-17 "up to 2.8x"; OpenLM.ai; vLLM issue 28947): speculative decoding is an ENGINE feature — scheduler multi-token slots, KV manager for draft+target, CPU-side spec_decode_worker doing rejection sampling. Establishes WALL A: the draft/verify loop cannot be built by GEMM interception under an unmodified vLLM; vLLM's 2.8x is a low-QPS figure that decays under load.
Conclusion: the prior pass's "deliverable, no-needs-model-training" tag is wrong on both axes (it needs a retrained checkpoint AND an engine-level control loop the substrate cannot author), and the gain it would chase (~1.3x for 7B) only exists at batch-1 on a special checkpoint, vanishing in the team's FP8 saturated vLLM regime.

research.summary: The quantization frontier splits cleanly along two axes relevant to CIPHER. (1) Precision of the GEMM math: FP8 (E4M3) is the Hopper ceiling and the team already measured it (~1.5x MBU on batch-1 decode, ~0.1-0.3% accuracy cost); FP4/MXFP4/NVFP4 give a real ~2-3x throughput-per-clock over FP8 but ONLY on Blackwell's 5th-gen tensor cores — on Hopper FP4 exists only as software emulation (FP4-to-FP8 upcast) with NO throughput win, so the answer to "does FP4 give >1.5x over FP8 on Hopper" is NO, it is Blackwell-only. (2) Weight-stream reduction for memory-bound decode: 4-bit weight-only (W4A16 via AWQ/GPTQ + Marlin) directly attacks the team's identified "more tokens per weight-stream" headroom, with ~0.05-0.2 PPL cost and up to ~2.8x end-to-end at batch 16 — but these all require a PRE-QUANTIZED, calibrated checkpoint and weight repacking, so they are NOT pure-substrate. KV-cache quantization (FP8-KV, KVQuant 2-3bit, W4A8KV4/QServe) is a real long-context win — FP8-KV doubles cache capacity (50% reduction) and in vLLM 2026 now delivers ~15% throughput + ~15% lower decode ITL on H100 above ~7k-token context — but it is a vLLM framework feature (kv_cache_dtype) tied to attention-kernel/cache layout, not something a GEMM-interposition layer cleanly owns. Net: only FP8-precision swap is genuinely pure-substrate, and the team has already proven its ceiling; everything with a bigger gain needs either Blackwell silicon, a pre-quantized checkpoint, or framework cooperation.

techniques.name: FP8 (E4M3) weight+activation GEMM (W8A8)
techniques.mechanism: Cast weights and activations to 8-bit float (E4M3) and run the GEMM on Hopper FP8 tensor cores; halves weight-stream bytes vs BF16 and doubles peak FLOPs. On batch-1 decode the win is bandwidth (fewer bytes per weight read), not compute.
techniques.reported_gain: ~0.1-0.3% accuracy drop typical; team's own measurement: ~1.5x MBU on batch-1 decode (caps ~54% MBU vs ~74% fp16). NVIDIA/community: ~4x memory reduction vs FP32, ~2x vs FP16; minimal MMLU/PPL loss. vLLM blog 2026: FP8 reasoning loss 'at most 1-2 points', long-context MRCR 97-98% of baseline AUC.

techniques.model_dependency: none for dynamic/RTN FP8 (on-the-fly cast at the intercepted GEMM); calibrated per-tensor scales (llm-compressor) improve accuracy but are optional
techniques.impl_cost: days-to-weeks (team has already built and measured this; it is the proven substrate baseline)

On Hopper there is NO native FP4 tensor core; FP4 can only be EMULATED via FP4-to-FP8 upcast, which yields zero throughput benefit (still runs at FP8 rates).

techniques.impl_cost: weeks-to-months on Blackwell (CUTLASS NVFP4 kernels); not applicable/no-win on the team's H100 fleet

techniques.mechanism: Migrate quantization difficulty from activations to weights via a per-channel smoothing scale, enabling full INT8/FP8 weight+activation GEMM with both operands quantized (true 2x compute, not just weight-stream).
techniques.reported_gain: Near-lossless W8A8 on OPT/Llama up to 175B-405B; drastically better than naive W8A8 PTQ. techniques.mechanism: Store K/V tensors as FP8 E4M3 (per-tensor or per-head scales) instead of FP16, halving cache bytes per token. BUT it is owned by the serving framework: vLLM controls the paged-KV layout and the attention kernel that reads it. A CUDA-driver GEMM-interposition layer does not own the KV cache or the FlashAttention kernel, so it cannot install this without vLLM cooperation.

assessment.technique: FP8 (E4M3) weight+activation GEMM (W8A8) via dynamic per-tensor cast at the intercepted GEMM
assessment.honest_gain:
Two distinct axes, do not conflate.

ACCURACY (real, small, but NOT "0.1-0.3%" for 7B): For dense 7B/8B, dynamic W8A8 FP8 is essentially lossless on easy tasks but loses ~0.5pp MMLU and ~2pp GSM8K. Measured (Red Hat/vLLM, Llama-3-8B): MMLU 66.6→66.27 (99.5%), GSM8K 75.96→73.99 (97.4%, ~2pp). arXiv 2502.01070: dynamic FP8 MMLU-CoT drop 0.5pp vs static 2.5pp -> dynamic/RTN is the right default, static calibration HURTS unless tuned. Long-context 8-bit ~0.8% avg drop (arXiv 2505.20276). Spheron states plainly: "For 7B models, expect 1-2% degradation." So the team's product copy should say ~0.5-2pp depending on task (math/reasoning/long-context worst), NOT "0.1-0.3%." Note the vLLM-2026 "97-98% AUC" number is FP8 KV-CACHE+ATTENTION, a different axis from W8A8 GEMM; the research pass conflated them.

THROUGHPUT/MBU — the headline "2x" is a tensor-core TFLOPS ceiling, NOT end-to-end serving gain, and is the wrong axis for batch-1 dense 7B:
- Batch-1 decode (memory-bound): the team's own ~1.5x MBU (fewer weight bytes/read) is the honest, defensible win and is the ONLY axis where FP8 clearly helps a single-stream 7B. This is bandwidth, not compute.
- Batched/saturated 7B-8B production: gain collapses. arXiv 2502.01070 measured FP8 decode at batch-64 on H100 = UNDER 25% over BF16. Offline-gen 8B = 1.07-1.33x (search-confirmed). The 1.4-1.8x figures are for 70B at large batch (Spheron/Red Hat), not 7B. So for THIS setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, batched) honest expectation is ~1.1-1.3x throughput, sometimes worse at low concurrency because the un-fused activation-cast overhead can make FP8 LOSE on latency/energy at small batch (arXiv 2502.01070, OSDI'25 park).
assessment.substrate_reality:
Intercept-only is NOT sufficient; this needs more than a GEMM-call swap, and the activation-cast overhead is the deliverability catch the research pass glossed.

What the substrate must actually build to deliver W8A8 (not just halve weight bytes):
1. Cast WEIGHTS to E4M3 once (cheap, can be done at load/first-touch on intercepted weight ptr). This alone gives the batch-1 weight-stream-bandwidth win — and is the one piece the substrate can do cleanly intercept-only.
2. Cast ACTIVATIONS to E4M3 on-the-fly every step, with a dynamic per-tensor scale computed from a live amax pass over the activation tensor. This is the hard part: it is an extra memory pass + amax reduction + cast kernel issued BEFORE the FP8 GEMM. Measured cost: quantization is ~20-30% of GEMM time on H800/H100 when un-fused (search-confirmed). At batch-1 this extra un-fused op can erase or invert the MBU win — exactly the regime this team cares about.
3. Output/epilogue dtype + dequant scale plumbing back to BF16 for the residual/LayerNorm path, and FP8 scale bookkeeping per tensor.

The team's substrate already GOT-patches cublasGemmEx and runs eager (per memory cipher-ra-realvllm-validation, cuBLAS-interceptor host REQUIRES eager, +51% eager tax vs cudagraph). Issuing the extra cast+amax kernels from the interposer is feasible (memory shows it already issues extra recompute kernels), but: (a) it inherits the eager tax, (b) the un-fused cast at batch-1 is precisely the overhead that can eat the 1.5x. The clean win (weight-only FP8 weight-stream) is really W8A16, not W8A8 — and W8A16 on Hopper needs a mixed-input GEMM kernel the substrate would have to supply (cuBLAS won't do W8A16-FP8 natively). True W8A8 needs the activation cast = framework/kernel cooperation for fusion to stay <3%. The team's prior measurements already landed FP8 at 1.05x iso-clock / 1.24x iso-power / +0.72% PPL via CUDA_INJECTION64_PATH (memory cipher-v0/mfu-batch-sweep) — consistent with this verdict: the substrate CAN turn it on, but the lift is the modest bandwidth/power number, not 2x.

Sources and what each established:

Per-channel/per-token = future work (not shipping).

This is the key "production-serving, not single-user" check — gain is real but ~1.1-1.25x at batch, not 2x.
- arXiv 2505.20276 (EMNLP 2025) long-context: 8-bit ~0.8% avg drop (vs 4-bit up to 59%) on Llama-3.1/Qwen-2.5 7B-72B. FP8 holds up on long context; 4-bit does not.
- Spheron FP8 blog (2026): tensor ceiling 1,979 vs 989 TFLOPS = 2x is a CEILING not serving throughput (their own caveat); real vLLM 70B serving 1.4-1.8x at large batch; "small batch -> gain smaller, memory-bound"; "for 7B models, expect 1-2% degradation."
- arXiv 2502.01070 v2 + OSDI'25 (usenix park) + search: activation must be quantized online before GEMM = non-trivial un-fused overhead; quant can be ~20-30% of GEMM time on H800/H100; at batch-1 FP8 can LOSE on latency/energy from un-fused ops + GPU underutilization.
- vLLM 2026 FP8-KV blog (97-98% AUC): this is KV-CACHE+ATTENTION FP8, a SEPARATE axis the research pass conflated with W8A8 GEMM.

Verdict rationale: gain is REAL and reproducible (accuracy small, batch-1 MBU ~1.5x genuine), but (1) headline 2x and "0.1-0.3% accuracy" are overstated for 7B-dense batched serving (real ~1.1-1.3x throughput, ~0.5-2pp accuracy), and (2) true W8A8 is NOT pure-intercept: the dynamic activation cast + amax + scale plumbing is framework/kernel work, and un-fused it can erase the batch-1 win. Pure-substrate cleanly delivers only the weight-side bandwidth (effectively W8A16, needing a mixed-input kernel), so "yes-pure-substrate" is too strong -> real-but-needs-model-or-framework (cooperation for fused activation quant to stay cheap).

technique.name: AWQ / GPTQ weight-only 4-bit (W4A16) + Marlin kernel
technique.mechanism: Quantize weights to INT4 (group-128) offline; AWQ scales salient channels to protect them, GPTQ uses Hessian-based error compensation. Marlin mixed-precision GEMM dequantizes 4-bit weights to 16-bit on the fly, overlapping dequant with FLOPs. Directly cuts the weight-stream bytes that bottleneck batch-1 decode — the team's 'more tokens per weight-stream' lever.
technique.reported_gain: AWQ: up to 3.9x vs FP16 (4090/Orin, TinyChat); WikiText-2 PPL degradation ~0.05-0.2 vs FP16 on Llama-family; 10x smaller calibration set than GPTQ. Marlin: ~3.9x vs FP16 on A10 large matrices, up to 2.8x end-to-end vs vLLM standard kernel at batch 16. Win shrinks as batch grows (becomes compute-bound).
technique.model_dependency: REQUIRES a pre-quantized, calibration-derived checkpoint (AWQ/GPTQ scales + INT4 repacked weights in Marlin layout). A GEMM-interposition layer cannot synthesize correct group scales on the fly without a calibration pass; it can host the Marlin GEMM but not produce the checkpoint.
technique.impl_cost: weeks (kernels exist in vLLM/Marlin; the gating cost is the offline quantization/calibration pipeline per model)

assessment.technique: AWQ / GPTQ weight-only 4-bit (W4A16) + Marlin mixed-precision GEMM kernel
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8 already on the table, PRODUCTION = batched/saturated serving), the honest expected throughput gain is roughly NEUTRAL-to-NEGATIVE, not 2.8-3.9x. The headline 3.9x (Marlin kernel) and 3x end-to-end were measured on an NVIDIA A10 — a bandwidth-starved 24GB card where the 7B weight stream dominates — at small batch (16-32). The technique is a memory-bandwidth lever; the team's own facts say batch-1 decode is exactly that regime. But the catch is the compute-bound crossover: Marlin's own paper/README state near-ideal ~3.87x holds only to batch 16-32, decaying to ~1.5x at batch 128 'as the problem becomes compute-bound.' Under saturated vLLM serving (continuous batching, prefill mixed in) you sit past the crossover. The decisive production datapoint: GPUStack's vLLM benchmark on a VRAM-ABUNDANT A100-80GB shows W4A16 REGRESSING throughput vs BF16 — AWQ -7.0% (9611 vs 10338 tok/s), GPTQ-Int4 -21.4% (8129 vs 10338) — because dequant overhead isn't paid back when you're not memory-constrained. A 7B model on H100 IS the VRAM-abundant case. W4A16 only posted +46% (AWQ) / +30% (GPTQ-Marlin) on a VRAM-CONSTRAINED RTX 4090. The 'BF16 or Death' paper confirms the dichotomy: W4A16 'consistently delivers highest gains for synchronous/single-stream' (1.5-2x latency, decode-bound) but flips in async/throughput deployment (one example: 0.3 vs 1.4 QPS, i.e. WORSE than FP16). So: REAL ~1.5-2x latency win for batch-1/low-QPS/latency-bound serving; LIKELY a throughput LOSS for saturated multi-tenant H100 serving — the opposite of the 2.8x claim once you account for batch and GPU class. Accuracy is good but not free: W4A16-INT on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct recovers 98.7% (OpenLLM-V1), 96.05% (V2), 93% (Arena-Hard), 99.9% (HumanEval); reasoning/long-context (GSM8K, RULER) can drop 1-3%+.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only does NOT suffice, and even with cooperation the substrate adds ~nothing over vLLM. AWQ/GPTQ REQUIRE an offline calibration pass: AWQ computes activation-aware per-channel salience scales from a calibration set; GPTQ runs Hessian-based error compensation; the result is INT4 weights repacked into Marlin's specific interleaved layout plus group-128 scale tensors. A CUDA GEMM-interposition substrate that GOT-patches cuBLAS/cutlass at runtime CANNOT synthesize correct group scales or Hessian corrections on the fly, and cannot repack the live FP16 weight tensors into Marlin layout without a calibration pass — confirmed: AWQ 'requires pre-computed statistics from a calibration dataset, cannot do on-the-fly quantization.' (bitsandbytes CAN quantize at load with no checkpoint, but runs ~4.5x slower than Marlin-AWQ — so the only on-the-fly path is the slow one.) What the substrate COULD do (host the Marlin FP16xINT4 GEMM by intercepting the linear call) is already done natively by vLLM/LLM-Compressor given a pre-quantized checkpoint — so interception is redundant, not enabling. Net: this needs a MODEL artifact (pre-quantized AWQ/GPTQ checkpoint), which is outside the substrate's 'no retrain / no fork / intercept-only' definition. It is 'model-cooperation' at minimum (someone ships the quantized checkpoint), and the serving win is captured by the existing framework, not by CIPHER's interception layer.
assessment.reasoning: Sources: (1) Marlin paper (arXiv:2408.11743) + GitHub IST-DASLab/marlin + Red Hat Developer article — peak 3.87x at batch 16-32 on A10, 'larger batchsizes up to 64-128 with gradually decreasing acceleration,' ~1.5x at batch 128 as compute-bound; vLLM end-to-end 3x on Llama-2-7B but on A10. (2) GPUStack 'Impact of Quantization on vLLM Inference Performance' — the production smoking gun: W4A16 regresses on VRAM-abundant A100-80GB (AWQ -7%, GPTQ-Int4 -21.4%) and only wins on VRAM-constrained 4090 (+46% AWQ); 'weight-only quantization causes performance degradation in TPS/TTFT/TPOT due to dequant overhead when VRAM is not constrained.' (3) 'Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death' (arXiv:2411.02355) — accuracy recovery numbers for W4A16 Llama-3.1-8B (98.7/96.05/93/99.9%) and the synchronous-vs-asynchronous dichotomy (best for single-stream decode, can be worse than FP16 in high-QPS throughput; 0.3 vs 1.4 QPS example). (4) SGLang/AWQ docs + theaiengineer/sesamedisk 2026 surveys + Keras AWQ guide — AWQ needs calibration set, cannot quantize on-the-fly; Marlin fuses dequant+matmul; bitsandbytes on-the-fly path ~4.5x slower. The research-pass's '2.8x end-to-end at batch 16' is a real number but it is the FAVORABLE corner (small batch, bandwidth-starved GPU); it does NOT survive the team's production constraints (H100 + saturated batching), and the deliverability claim 'no-needs-model-training' glosses the mandatory calibration/repack checkpoint that the intercept-only substrate cannot produce.

technique.name: SmoothQuant W8A8 (activation outlier migration)
technique.mechanism: Migrate quantization difficulty from activations to weights via a per-channel smoothing scale, enabling full INT8/FP8 weight+activation GEMM with both operands quantized (true 2x compute, not just weight-stream).
technique.reported_gain: Near-lossless W8A8 on OPT/Llama up to 175B-405B; drastically better than naive W8A8 PTQ. Enables high inference speed via W8A8 but slightly lower weight-only accuracy than AWQ/GPTQ. (Specific speedup is hardware/kernel dependent; the win overlaps the team's measured FP8 ceiling.)
technique.model_dependency: needs an offline calibration pass to compute per-channel smoothing scales and fold them into weights; the activation-side scale must be baked in, so not deliverable by pure interception without a checkpoint transform
technique.impl_cost: weeks (calibration + scale-folding pipeline)

assessment.technique: SmoothQuant W8A8 (activation outlier migration / per-channel smoothing into weights)
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8 already in hand): ~0 incremental, and likely negative on accuracy. SmoothQuant enables INT8 W8A8 (true both-operand 8-bit compute, the real win vs naive W8A8 PTQ), but on Hopper INT8 and FP8 tensor cores have IDENTICAL peak throughput (3026 TFLOPS dense / 3958 sparse for both INT8 and FP8 — NVIDIA H100 datasheet). So W8A8-INT delivers no compute speedup over the FP8 path the team already measured. Compute-bound MFU is framework-pointwise-bound at ~68% regardless of 8-bit format, so the GEMM precision is not the binding constraint. In the memory-bound batch-1 decode regime the team cares about, an 8-bit GEMM does nothing extra — the bottleneck is the weight stream, and W8A8 reads the same 8-bit weights as FP8 weight-only (no MBU advantage; team already has ~54% MBU FP8 GEMV path). Where INT8 W8A8 helps at all is the compute-bound batched/prefill regime, and even there it merely TIES FP8 on throughput while LOSING on accuracy. Real production speedup data (Databricks H100 blog): FP8 gives ~2.2x throughput vs FP16 via 2x batch + ~10% TPOT at high batch / ~30% at batch<8, and they explicitly chose FP8 OVER INT8 activation quant because 'FP8 tends to produce more accurate models than INT8.' Accuracy ('Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death', ACL 2025 / arXiv 2411.02355): W8A8-FP (FP8) is essentially lossless (~100% recovery, within margin of error); W8A8-INT (SmoothQuant+GPTQ) is 1-3% degraded (Open LLM V2 min per-task 97.8% on 405B). SmoothQuant does NOT match FP8 even with GPTQ pairing. The 405B eval (arXiv 2409.11055) reports SmoothQuant 'performs poorly' / 'significant accuracy drops' on Llama-3.1-405B due to high activation ranges. Net: SmoothQuant W8A8 is a 2022-2023 A100/pre-FP8-hardware win (A100 had no FP8, so INT8 W8A8 was the only true-2x-compute path); on FP8-native H100 it is strictly dominated by the FP8 the team already has.
assessment.substrate_reality: NOT deliverable by the substrate as defined (intercept-only, no retrain, no vLLM fork). SmoothQuant's per-channel smoothing scale s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) is computed on a CALIBRATION pass and then FOLDED OFFLINE into the weights — and critically, the activation-side reciprocal scale is mathematically migrated into the PREVIOUS layer's weights (LayerNorm/prior-linear) so that at runtime activations arrive already-smoothed with NO runtime scaling op. This is a checkpoint transform: LLM Compressor's SmoothQuant modifier docs state it 'manipulates the weights of the model' and 'can only be used in one-shot, not during training,' producing a prequantized compressed-tensors safetensors checkpoint that vLLM loads via metadata. A GOT-patch / cuBLAS-intercept substrate that runs under unmodified vLLM with the original checkpoint cannot synthesize this: it would have to (a) run a calibration pass, (b) rewrite the weights of layer L AND the preceding layer L-1 (cross-layer fold), and (c) bake activation scales into the stored weights — i.e., produce a new checkpoint. Intercepting the GEMM call at runtime is too late and wrong-place: the smoothing must already be in the operands. The MODEL DEP note in the prompt is correct and the research-pass 'no-needs-model-training' flag is the relevant overclaim — it is true there is no gradient training, but there IS a mandatory offline checkpoint transform (calibration + weight rewrite), which is exactly the thing the substrate-as-defined cannot do. If the team allowed a one-time offline checkpoint-prep tool that ships an SmoothQuant'd model to vLLM, that is 'needs-framework/checkpoint-change,' not pure interception — and even then it buys nothing over loading an FP8 checkpoint on H100.
assessment.reasoning: Sources: (1) Accuracy critique — 'Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death? Accuracy-Performance Trade-Offs in LLM Quantization' (arXiv 2411.02355v3 / ACL 2025 long paper): W8A8-FP essentially lossless; W8A8-INT (SmoothQuant+GPTQ) 1-3% degraded, ~99% V2 recovery with min 97.8% (MMLU-Pro 405B); states SmoothQuant 'substantially improved results but did not match FP8.' (2) 405B comprehensive eval (arXiv 2409.11055): 'SmoothQuant exhibits significant accuracy drops in Llama-3.1-405B due to ineffective handling of high activation ranges'; FP8 most stable. (3) Production H100 serving — Databricks 'Serving Quantized LLMs on NVIDIA H100' blog: FP8 2.2x throughput vs FP16 (via 2x batch), ~10% TPOT high-batch / ~30% batch<8; they DELIBERATELY avoided INT8 activation quant in favor of FP8 for accuracy; INT8 weight-only gives no speedup above batch~8 (compute stays FP16) and can be slower on TTFT. (4) Hardware — NVIDIA H100 datasheet: INT8 and FP8 tensor cores both 3026 TFLOPS dense / 3958 sparse, i.e., NO INT8 throughput advantage on Hopper. (5) Deliverability — mit-han-lab/smoothquant + paper (arXiv 2211.10438): smoothing factor 'computed offline from calibration set and merged into weights before quantization,' fused into the previous layer offline; LLM Compressor SmoothQuant modifier docs: 'manipulates the weights... one-shot only,' producing a compressed-tensors prequantized checkpoint vLLM loads. The original SmoothQuant 1.56x speedup / 1.9x memory numbers were on A100-class hardware (no native FP8), which is why the technique mattered then and is superseded by FP8 now. All four skeptical axes confirm: gain is real-but-single-era (pre-FP8 hardware), does NOT hold as an advantage in batched H100 serving (FP8 ties or beats it), is NOT intercept-deliverable (mandatory offline cross-layer weight fold), and the honest gain for this team over their existing FP8 is ~0 with worse accuracy.

technique.name: QServe W4A8KV4 (QoQ) — 4-bit weight, 8-bit act, 4-bit KV co-design
technique.mechanism: Quantize weights to 4-bit, activations to 8-bit, KV cache to 4-bit, with register-level parallelism to hide INT4 dequant in the GEMM main loop. Targets large-batch cloud serving where prior INT4 methods lost gains to 20-90% dequant overhead.
technique.reported_gain: Llama-3-8B throughput +1.2x on A100, +1.4x on L40S; Qwen1.5-72B +2.4x on A100, +3.5x on L40S vs TensorRT-LLM; avg 2.36x over TRT-LLM v0.9.0 on L40S, 1.68x on A100. Beats W4A4 (Atom) which suffers partial-sum dequant overhead.
technique.model_dependency: requires the full QoQ quantized checkpoint (4-bit weights + activation/KV scales) plus the QServe runtime/kernels; it is a system co-design, not a precision swap a substrate can apply to an unmodified model
technique.impl_cost: months (quantization algorithm + custom kernels + serving integration)

assessment.technique: QServe W4A8KV4 (QoQ) — 4-bit weight / 8-bit activation / 4-bit KV co-design (MLSys'25, MIT Han Lab / OmniServe)
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8 baseline): honest expected gain is roughly ZERO to NEGATIVE, and the substrate cannot deliver it at all. (1) NO H100 number exists in the paper — gains are A100 (1.2x) and L40S (1.4x) for Llama-3-8B, vs a now-18-months-stale TensorRT-LLM v0.9.0 (Apr 2024) FP16 baseline, NOT vs FP8. The headline 2.36x avg / 72B 2.4-3.5x is mostly L40S/large-model and does not transfer to a 7B on H100. (2) On Hopper the INT4 register-level dequant path that QoQ relies on degrades: Hopper has no INT4 tensor-core path (wgmma lacks INT4; INT4 lowers to IMAD on CUDA cores), and TensorRT-LLM issue #3977 (closed 'not a bug') shows QServe-w4a8 collapsing to ~FP16/W16A16-level efficiency on H20-class Hopper silicon, with per-token quant/cast ops dominating. (3) The dequant overhead QoQ claimed to eliminate was re-opened by LiquidGEMM (arXiv 2509.01229, Sep 2025): QServe's vadd-based subtraction is ~21% of warp stalls on LLaMA2-7B FFN; LiquidGEMM reports up to 2.90x over QServe's W4A8 kernel and 1.12-1.63x over TensorRT-LLM — QServe's own kernel is now superseded. The Llama-3-8B gain vs a modern FP8/W4A8-marlin vLLM on H100 is unverified and plausibly <1x. (4) Accuracy cost: +0.27 WikiText2 PPL vs W4A16 AWQ (6.81 vs 6.54), +0.67 vs FP16 (6.14) on Llama-3-8B — fails this team's quality bar history (they reject ~+0.7% PPL FP8).
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only does NOT suffice — non-starter for CIPHER as defined. QoQ is an end-to-end SYSTEM CO-DESIGN, not a precision swap at the GEMM-call boundary: it needs (a) the offline QoQ checkpoint — 4-bit weights with progressive two-level quant scales, plus per-channel/group activation scales and SmoothAttention KV scales from a calibration pass (offline model preparation the substrate by definition does not do — 'does NOT retrain models'); (b) QServe's own runtime/kernels (OmniServe) with custom register-level INT4 dequant fused into the INT8 GEMM main loop and compute-aware weight reorder — the substrate would have to REPLACE cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM with a bespoke W4A8 kernel AND change the KV-cache layout to 4-bit, i.e., re-implement and own the GEMM + attention/KV path, not merely GOT-patch a call. GOT-patching a cublasGemmEx call to a QServe kernel is impossible: at that seam the inputs are FP16/FP8 activations + FP16/FP8 weights with the wrong layout and no 4-bit scales — the substrate has nothing to feed a W4A8 kernel. It also never landed in vLLM (issue #4763 closed 'not planned'), so there is no 'runs under unmodified vLLM' path — you must run the OmniServe stack, which is forking the serving runtime. Verdict: needs offline model quantization + replacement runtime/kernels + KV-layout change. Pure-substrate delivery is not achievable.
assessment.reasoning: Sources: QServe paper arXiv 2405.04532 / MLSys'25 (hanlab.mit.edu/projects/qserve) — A100+L40S ONLY, no H100; baseline TensorRT-LLM v0.9.0 (Apr 18 2024); 'maximum achievable throughput' = max batch within fixed memory (batch tuned per system, seq 1024/512); W4A8 GEMM on INT8 tensor cores with dequant pushed to CUDA cores. Llama-3-8B PPL: FP16 6.14, W8A8-SQ 6.28, W4A16-AWQ 6.54, W4A8KV4-QoQ 6.81. Critiques: (1) NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM issue #3977 'Qserve-w4a8 Shows Lower Computational Efficiency on H20' — QServe schemes 'achieving results comparable to w16a16 (FP16 baseline)' on Hopper-class H20, root cause excessive per-token quant/cast, labeled 'not a bug'. (2) LiquidGEMM arXiv 2509.01229 (Sep 2025) — QServe dequant overflow forces vadd (non-native, ~dozen ops) = 21% of warp stalls; LiquidGEMM up to 2.90x over QServe W4A8 kernel, 1.12-1.63x over TensorRT-LLM, up to 4.94x e2e over QServe; tested H800/A100/H100 roofline. (3) Hopper INT4 limitation corroborated: wgmma has no INT4 tensor-core support, INT4 lowers to IMAD/CUDA cores on Hopper, so the INT4-dequant calculus that wins on Ampere/Ada disfavors H100. (4) vLLM issue #4763 (W4A8KV4/QServe) opened May 2024, CLOSED not planned/stale — never integrated; vLLM's own W4A8 is a separate marlin path (PR #24722, VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE=int8) reporting 2.24x over FP16 / 1.25x over W4A16, unrelated to QServe and itself a model-prep + kernel feature, not substrate-applicable. Net: gain is real on its 2024 A100/L40S-vs-TRT-v0.9.0 config but is single-vendor-stack, superseded on the kernel, untested/architecturally-disfavored on H100, and structurally undeliverable by an intercept-only substrate.

research.summary: The state of the art splits cleanly along the team's own findings. (1) Attention/GEMM KERNEL LIBRARIES (FlashAttention-3, FlashInfer, Flash-Decoding, Machete, SplitK) are genuine wins but they lift the COMPUTE-bound prefill MFU (FA3 hits 75% of H100 FP16 peak vs FA2's ~35%) or the attention portion of long-context decode; they do little for batch-1 short-context decode, which is memory-bound and dominated by weight streaming, not attention FLOPs. These are real kernel-swaps-behind-an-intercepted-call and are the most substrate-deliverable items here — but modern vLLM/SGLang already call them, so marginal gain over an up-to-date stack is small. (2) The biggest decode-latency lever is MEGAKERNELS (Hazy Research: 2.5x vs vLLM on Llama-1B batch-1 H100; Mirage/MPK: 1.2-6.7x, but a measured-on-A100 per-token number of only ~14% at 14.5ms->12.5ms). Critically, megakernels win by raising memory-bandwidth utilization from ~50% to ~78% (NOT MFU) and they fuse the ENTIRE forward pass into one launch — they replace the framework's execution model rather than swap one kernel behind one intercepted GEMM. (3) Fusing the pointwise overhead that caps single-GPU MFU at ~68% yields only single-digit gains (vLLM torch.compile activation+quant fusion: up to 8%; AllReduce+RMSNorm: up to 15% but that is multi-GPU collective), and it is framework/compiler-owned, matching the team's prior finding that vLLM rejects external graph mutation. Bottom line for a substrate: kernel-library swaps are deliverable but largely already done; the megakernel decode win is real and large but is a framework-replacement, not a substrate kernel-swap.

techniques.name: FlashAttention-3 (FA3) Hopper attention
techniques.mechanism: Warp-specialized async pipeline overlapping WGMMA tensor-core matmul with TMA loads and softmax, plus FP8 block-quantization with incoherent processing, to saturate Hopper tensor cores on the attention GEMMs.
techniques.reported_gain: 740 TFLOPs FP16 = 75% of H100 peak (vs FlashAttention-2 at ~35%), 1.5-2.0x faster than FA2; ~1.2 PFLOPs FP8 with 2.6x lower numerical error than baseline FP8 attention. Benchmarks are long-sequence prefill/training, not batch-1 decode.
techniques.axis: MFU (prefill/long-context attention); negligible for batch-1 short-context decode which is memory-bound
techniques.model_dependency: none (FP8 mode benefits from per-tensor scales but FP16 path needs nothing)
techniques.impl_cost: days to weeks (intercept attention call, dispatch to the existing FA3 kernel; must match KV layout/RoPE/masking semantics exactly)

techniques.name: Flash-Decoding (split-KV attention)
techniques.mechanism: Adds a parallelization dimension over the KV-sequence length: splits keys/values into chunks, computes partial attention per chunk in parallel via FlashAttention, then a small rescale/combine reduction recovers the exact result, keeping all SMs busy at batch-1 when context is long.
techniques.reported_gain: Up to 8x faster generation for very long sequences (Stanford CRFM / PyTorch blog); benefit only material when context length is large (helps long-context decode, not short-context).
techniques.axis: latency / throughput for long-context batch-1 decode (fills idle SMs)
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: days (already shipped in xFormers/FlashInfer/vLLM; for a substrate it is intercept-attention-and-dispatch)

techniques.name: FlashInfer (customizable attention engine / kernel library)
techniques.mechanism: JIT-compiled, block-sparse/composable KV-cache attention templates with a load-balanced Stream-K scheduler (atomics-free, CUDAGraph-compatible, deterministic); covers paged attention, GQA, fused-RoPE.
techniques.reported_gain: 29-69% inter-token-latency reduction vs compiler-backend baselines; 28-30% latency reduction long-context; 13-17% speedup for parallel generation on H100 (FlashInfer paper, arXiv 2501.01005). Now the default attention backend in vLLM/SGLang/MLC.
techniques.axis: latency / throughput (attention path)
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: weeks (it is a drop-in kernel library; a substrate would dispatch intercepted attention to it. But since vLLM already integrates it, marginal gain over an updated vLLM is small)

techniques.name: Low-latency megakernel (Hazy Research, Llama-1B)
techniques.mechanism: Fuses the ENTIRE forward pass into a single persistent on-GPU 'interpreter' kernel that distributes ~7 fused instruction types across SMs, paging weights through shared memory so weight loads never stall compute — eliminates kernel-boundary stalls and the ~1.3-2.1us per-kernel launch cost.
techniques.reported_gain: ~2.5x faster than vLLM and >1.5x faster than SGLang for Llama-1B batch-1 decode on H100 (>3.5x vs vLLM on B200). Lifts HBM bandwidth utilization from at most ~50% to 78% on H100. Win is memory-bandwidth, not MFU.
techniques.axis: latency / MBU (batch-1 decode)
techniques.model_dependency: none to the model weights, BUT requires a whole-model compiler/runtime that owns the entire forward pass (not a per-call kernel swap)
techniques.impl_cost: months (it is a new execution engine; a GEMM-interposition substrate cannot reconstruct a whole-model single launch from individually intercepted calls — it replaces vLLM's executor)

techniques.name: Mirage Persistent Kernel / MPK (megakernel compiler)
techniques.mechanism: Compiler+runtime that auto-transforms a tensor program into one megakernel using an SM-level dependency graph enabling cross-operator software pipelining and fine-grained overlap; kernels generated by the Mirage superoptimizer. Provides its own runtime.
techniques.reported_gain: 1.2x-6.7x end-to-end latency reduction (paper abstract, range across configs/GPUs); concretely measured ~13.8% per-token on a single A100 (14.5ms->12.5ms, theoretical floor ~10ms). Replaces the serving framework rather than integrating.
techniques.axis: latency (decode)
techniques.model_dependency: none to weights; needs the model expressed to the MPK compiler and run under MPK's runtime (~dozens of lines), supplanting vLLM
techniques.impl_cost: months (own compiler + runtime; not a substrate kernel-swap; no MoE/dynamic support yet)

techniques.name: CUDA graphs (launch-overhead elimination)
techniques.mechanism: Captures the decode kernel sequence once and replays the whole graph per step, removing per-kernel CPU launch and stream-sync overhead (~1.3us/kernel captured vs ~2.1us/kernel on streams).
techniques.reported_gain: ~28% reduction in per-iteration decode overhead from kernel-launch + stream-sync elimination (vLLM docs / community); it is the baseline the team already runs (their eager-host detector pays a measured +51% tax for being eager, i.e. cudagraph is ~2.05x over eager).
techniques.axis: latency / throughput (decode, launch-bound regime)
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: n/a for substrate (the team measured that external structural mutation of vLLM's owned decode graph is rejected — cudagraph is framework-owned; capture must be authored by vLLM)

techniques.name: torch.compile pointwise fusion (RMSNorm/SiLU/RoPE/quant)
techniques.mechanism: Inductor + vLLM custom passes fuse memory-bound pointwise ops (activation+quantize, RMSNorm+quant, attention+quant) into single kernels via piecewise compilation, cutting redundant HBM round-trips that cap MFU.

Single-digit, memory-bound-overhead origin not launch overhead.

techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: n/a for substrate (fusion happens at the torch.fx graph level inside vLLM/Inductor; a GEMM-interposition layer sees opaque post-fusion kernels and cannot author new fused kernels into vLLM's graph — matches team's prior capture-illegal finding). Headroom in fusing the ~68%-MFU pointwise tail is real but capped at single-digit % and is framework-owned.

technique.name: FlashAttention-3 (FA3) Hopper attention
technique.mechanism: Warp-specialized async pipeline overlapping WGMMA tensor-core matmul with TMA loads and softmax, plus FP8 block-quantization with incoherent processing, to saturate Hopper tensor cores on the attention GEMMs.
