technique.axis: MFU (prefill/long-context attention); negligible for batch-1 short-context decode which is memory-bound
technique.model_dependency: none (FP8 mode benefits from per-tensor scales but FP16 path needs nothing)
technique.impl_cost: days to weeks (intercept attention call, dispatch to the existing FA3 kernel; must match KV layout/RoPE/masking semantics exactly)

assessment.technique: FlashAttention-3 (FA3) Hopper warp-specialized attention + FP8 block-quant attention
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, batch-1/low-batch decode): ~0% incremental gain, because vLLM ALREADY runs FA3 as the default attention backend on Hopper (SM90) with no flag (vLLM docs: "FA4 on SM100+, FA3 on SM90, FA2 otherwise"). The baseline is already FA3 — there is nothing for an interposition substrate to add. The headline numbers do NOT apply to this regime: 740 TFLOPs/75%-peak/1.5-2.0x over FA2 is measured at head-dim 128, seq 8K, fwd+bwd (long-sequence PREFILL/TRAINING, a compute-bound regime) per the FA3 paper/Tri Dao blog. Batch-1 decode is memory-bound (KV-cache load), which the FA3 authors themselves call out as FA3's weak spot (parallelizes over query length; needs Split-KV/Flash-Decoding for parallelism). A real third-party benchmark (Dao-AILab issue #1572) shows FA3 batch decode 2.6-3.3x SLOWER than FlashInfer on MHA across KV lengths 128-32000 — so even attention-kernel choice within decode does not favor FA3. Net for short-context 7B decode serving: attention is also a minority of decode latency (~50% at most, batch/seq dependent; linear GEMMs/KV-stream dominate at small batch), and per Amdahl any attention-kernel win is diluted. The only place a remaining gain exists is FP8 ATTENTION on LONG context, which is a different lever (see substrate_reality).
assessment.substrate_reality: The substrate would have to MAKE vLLM use FA3 — but vLLM already does, by default, on H100. GOT-patching/intercepting cuBLAS or attention calls to force FA3 is redundant with the framework's own default, so "pure-substrate delivers FA3" is double-counting an existing baseline, not a new win. Intercept-only cannot improve on an already-FA3 attention call: the FA3 kernel is selected and launched by vLLM's FlashAttention backend; the substrate has no faster kernel to swap in (and a hand-tuned kernel ties cutlass at best per this team's own findings). The one genuinely-unbuilt lever is FP8 ATTENTION (the 1.2 PFLOPs / 2.6x-lower-error part). That is NOT pure-substrate and NOT free: (a) it is OPT-IN in vLLM (FA3 default KV-cache types are auto/fp16/bf16; FP8 attention needs the FP8-KV-cache backend path / explicit config — a framework change, not a driver intercept); (b) the measured end-to-end serving gain is long-context-only — Llama-3.1-8B ~14.9% higher output throughput / 13% faster runtime, but break-even is ~7k tokens (below that FP8 attention is net-neutral or negative), so it does nothing for short-context 7B decode; (c) accuracy is fragile on real models — naive FP8/INT8 attention causes severe degradation (Llama2 MMLU collapses to ~25.5% random-level with INT8 attention; real K matrices have channel-wise outliers), which is exactly why SageAttention/Hadamard smoothing exists. Incoherent processing helps synthetic-outlier error 2.6x but is not a free correctness guarantee on arbitrary served models — so it edges toward needing model/calibration cooperation, not intercept-only.
assessment.reasoning: Sources verified by web search/fetch: (1) FA3 headline numbers and regime — Tri Dao blog (tridao.me/blog/2024/flash3) and arXiv 2407.08608: FA3 FP16 "up to 740 TFLOPS, 75% utilization" vs FA2 ~350 TFLOPS/35%, "1.5-2.0x faster," FP8 "close to 1.2 PFLOPS, 2.6x smaller error," all at head-dim 128 / seq 8K / fwd+bwd; blog gives NO decode/batch-1/KV-cache numbers. (2) Decode is FA3's weak spot — FA3 NeurIPS paper text: decode is "memory-bound," FA3 "parallelizes over the query sequence length...can suffer from lack of parallelism for decoding," needs Split-KV. (3) Real decode benchmark — Dao-AILab/flash-attention issue #1572: FA3 batch decode 2.6-3.3x slower than FlashInfer on MHA (KV 128->32000). (4) vLLM already ships FA3 by default on Hopper — vLLM attention-backends docs: priority "FLASH_ATTN, FLASHINFER, ..." and "FA4 on SM100+, FA3 on SM90, FA2 otherwise," no flag required; FP8 attention is opt-in (FA3 KV-cache types: auto/float16/bfloat16). (5) FP8 attention end-to-end gain and its long-context-only nature — vLLM FP8-KV-cache blog (2026-04-22): Llama-3.1-8B "14.9% higher output throughput, 13.0% faster total runtime," ITL slope 54% of BF16, but break-even ~7k tokens; FP8 "free" with scale=1.0 for many models but some need calibration. (6) FP8-attention accuracy fragility on real models — SageAttention paper (arXiv 2410.02367) and CyberInsist comparison: naive FA3-FP8 produces blurry images / Llama2 INT8 MMLU ~25.5%; real K channel-wise outliers, smoothing needed. Conclusion: the original "yes-pure-substrate" research pass conflated FA3-the-kernel (already vLLM default; nothing to deliver) with FA3-FP8-attention (a long-context, opt-in, accuracy-fragile lever that is framework+possibly-calibration work, not intercept-only) — and applied a prefill/training compute-bound number to a memory-bound decode setup it does not describe.

technique.name: Flash-Decoding (split-KV attention)
technique.mechanism: Adds a parallelization dimension over the KV-sequence length: splits keys/values into chunks, computes partial attention per chunk in parallel via FlashAttention, then a small rescale/combine reduction recovers the exact result, keeping all SMs busy at batch-1 when context is long.
technique.reported_gain: Up to 8x faster generation for very long sequences (Stanford CRFM / PyTorch blog); benefit only material when context length is large (helps long-context decode, not short-context).
technique.axis: latency / throughput for long-context batch-1 decode (fills idle SMs)
technique.model_dependency: none
technique.impl_cost: days (already shipped in xFormers/FlashInfer/vLLM; for a substrate it is intercept-attention-and-dispatch)

assessment.technique: Flash-Decoding (split-KV / split-K attention for long-context decode)
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, Mistral/Llama-7B dense GQA, vLLM, FP8) the honest incremental gain is ~0%, because the technique is ALREADY the baseline. vLLM's FlashAttention backend (FA2/FA3) ships split-KV/flash-decoding by default with a num_splits heuristic, so there is nothing to add. The headline "up to 8x" is a single-config number: CodeLlama-34B, batch=1, seqlen 512->64k, where the attention MICROBENCHMARK is up to ~50x faster (e.g. seqlen=65536: FA2 2300us -> Flash-Decoding 64us per PyTorch/CRFM blog Oct-2023) and that flows to ~8x END-TO-END only because at batch-1/64k context attention dominates step latency. None of those conditions match 7B-dense vLLM serving: (a) batched/saturated serving fills SMs from the batch dimension, collapsing the underutilization flash-decoding fixes; (b) 7B GQA has only 8 KV heads, already cutting KV-read bandwidth and SM-tile starvation; (c) typical serving contexts are far short of 64k. The only LIVE residual tuning win is the 2026 FA3 sequence-aware split-heuristic paper (arXiv 2604.00028): +21-24% on the DECODE ATTENTION KERNEL on H100, but ONLY for HKV in {1,2} (MQA/few-KV-head) and explicitly 1.00x (no change) for HKV=8 — which is exactly Llama/Mistral-7B. And even that 21-24% is kernel-local, requires precomputed scheduler_metadata (else drops to 1.0-1.05x), and is a fraction of end-to-end step time. Net for this team: nothing to harvest.
assessment.substrate_reality: The substrate as defined (GOT-patch / intercept cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM and CUDA kernels, classifier, cross-process, clocks/power, under unmodified vLLM, no model retrain, no vLLM fork) CANNOT deliver flash-decoding, for two independent reasons. (1) Wrong call site: attention is computed by vLLM's own FlashAttention kernel (flash_attn_varlen_func, FA2/FA3) — a fused CUDA kernel, NOT a cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM. The substrate intercepts GEMMs; the attention op is not a GEMM the interposer sees. The team's own prior measurement already states this exactly: 'attention=FlashAttn NOT cuBLAS -> uncovered' (cipher-ra-realvllm-validation). So intercept-only does not reach the kernel. (2) Already done: even if it could reach it, the kernel ALREADY does split-KV by default — there is no slower baseline to replace. The only lever left (the FA3 split-heuristic override) means writing num_splits / scheduler_metadata into FlashAttention's launch parameters, i.e. cooperating with the vLLM attention backend's scheduling — model/framework cooperation the intercept-only substrate does not have. Could the substrate hijack the FlashAttention kernel launch via its kernel-interception path and rewrite the grid/splits? Only by replacing vLLM's attention kernel with the substrate's own implementation — that is effectively forking the attention backend, which violates the intercept-only/no-fork line and would have to re-derive vLLM's paged-KV block table. Intercept-only does NOT suffice; this is a 'needs-vLLM/kernel cooperation' lever with ~0 payoff for 7B GQA anyway.
assessment.reasoning: Sources: PyTorch blog 'Flash-Decoding for long-context inference' (pytorch.org/blog/flash-decoding/) and Stanford CRFM (crfm.stanford.edu/2023/10/12/flashdecoding.html) — the 'up to 8x' is CodeLlama-34B, batch=1, seqlen up to 64k, end-to-end; the underlying attention microbenchmark is 'up to 50x faster than FlashAttention' (e.g. seqlen=65536 FA2 2300.6us -> Flash-Decoding 64.4us), and the blog states explicitly the regime is batch-size-1 with long context, where vanilla FA2 'uses less than 1% of the GPU'. Already-in-vLLM: vLLM FlashAttention/FlashInfer integration (DeepWiki vllm 8.2; PR #3648 'Use flash-attn for decoding') uses flash_attn_varlen_func with split-KV and a max_num_splits / 'max number splits for cuda graph decode' config — i.e. flash-decoding is the default decode path, not an add-on. Production-serving / GQA caveat: arXiv 2604.00028 'Sequence-Aware Split Heuristic to Mitigate SM Underutilization in FA3 Low-Head-Count Decoding' (2026) — FA3 already does split-KV but aborts splitting when LK<=512; the override yields +21-24% but ONLY for HKV in {1,2}, and is explicitly 1.00x (unchanged) for HKV=8, with gains contingent on precomputed scheduler_metadata (else 1.0-1.05x). Batch caveat corroborated by Together.ai/CRFM ('with batch size 1, FlashAttention uses <1% of the GPU') and the general result that at higher batch the attention parallelizes over the batch dimension so the SM-starvation flash-decoding fixes no longer exists; multiple serving analyses note that at small batch latency is GEMM/linear-dominated and attention only dominates as context AND batch grow. Mistral/Llama-7B use 8 KV heads (GQA), placing them squarely in the HKV=8 'no win' bucket and with already-reduced KV bandwidth. Substrate non-coverage corroborated directly by the team's own measurement that vLLM attention runs on FlashAttn, not cuBLAS, so the GEMM interposer never sees it. Conclusion: gain is real but single-config and already-baseline; for H100/7B-dense-GQA/vLLM it is not-for-this-setup and not substrate-deliverable.

technique.name: FlashInfer (customizable attention engine / kernel library)
technique.mechanism: JIT-compiled, block-sparse/composable KV-cache attention templates with a load-balanced Stream-K scheduler (atomics-free, CUDAGraph-compatible, deterministic); covers paged attention, GQA, fused-RoPE.
technique.reported_gain: 29-69% inter-token-latency reduction vs compiler-backend baselines; 28-30% latency reduction long-context; 13-17% speedup for parallel generation on H100 (FlashInfer paper, arXiv 2501.01005). Now the default attention backend in vLLM/SGLang/MLC.
technique.model_dependency: none
technique.impl_cost: weeks (it is a drop-in kernel library; a substrate would dispatch intercepted attention to it. But since vLLM already integrates it, marginal gain over an updated vLLM is small)

assessment.technique: FlashInfer (customizable attention engine / JIT block-sparse paged-attention kernel library)
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's exact setup (H100/SM90, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8): expected gain is roughly ZERO to NEGATIVE, not 29-69%. The headline 29-69% inter-token-latency reduction is measured vs SGLang's Triton compiler backend (arXiv 2501.01005, SGLang v0.3.4) — NOT vs the production default. On H100/SM90 vLLM auto-selects FlashAttention-3 (FA4 on Blackwell, FA3 on Hopper, FA2 otherwise); FlashInfer is only an auto fallback on Blackwell SM100, not on Hopper. Against FA3, independent benchmarks show FlashInfer tied or slower: vLLM issue #9471 (Llama-3.1-8B-FP8, H100, batch=64, 1024in/1024out): FlashAttention 6003 tok/s vs FlashInfer 5020 tok/s = FlashInfer ~16% SLOWER for exactly the FP8/7B/H100 case this team runs. vLLM issue #6617 (Qwen2-72B-128k long-context, A100): improvement "quite marginal," closed not-planned. The other paper numbers are also soft baselines: 28-30% long-context is vs FlashAttention's UNFUSED kernel (Streaming-LLM/Vicuna-13B); 13-17% parallel-gen is an ablation vs FlashInfer-WITHOUT-composable-formats (MLC-Engine), not vs FA at all. Where FlashInfer genuinely wins (and these are real): skewed/variable-length batches 70-83% BW util vs ~45% for FA, and certain GQA/batch-decode cases (e.g. H20 batch decode beats FA3, Dao-AILab issue #1572) — but these are regime-specific, not the uniform short-context batched FP8 decode this team is optimizing, and FlashInfer 0.2 already integrates FA3 templates so the kernel gap on Hopper prefill has largely closed.
assessment.substrate_reality: The substrate as defined (GOT-patch / intercept cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM calls, classifier, cross-process, DVFS, under unmodified vLLM, no vLLM fork) CANNOT deliver FlashInfer. Two hard blockers: (1) WRONG INTERCEPTION SURFACE. FlashInfer is an attention kernel library, not a GEMM call. vLLM runs attention through a dedicated FlashAttention/FlashInfer kernel path, which the team's own measurements already flagged as 'attention=FlashAttn NOT cuBLAS -> uncovered' by their cuBLAS/cublasGemmEx interceptor (cipher-ra-realvllm-validation). GOT-patching cuBLAS does not touch the attention path, so there is nothing for the substrate to swap. (2) IT'S A CONFIG FLAG + SOURCE-WIRED API, NOT A DRIVER PRIMITIVE. FlashInfer is selected by VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER (or auto-selection logic in vLLM source) and requires explicit per-step plan()/run() Python API calls that vLLM's attention backend module must issue (the plan stage is deliberately NOT CUDAGraph-captured). Intercept-only at the driver level cannot inject a plan/run scheduling protocol into vLLM's Python attention dispatch without forking/modifying vLLM. The honest 'substrate action' here is trivial and non-novel: set an env var / launch flag (VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER) at process spawn — which the team's cross-process classifier could technically do — but (a) that is config management, not interposition, and (b) it would make things WORSE on H100 by overriding FA3 with a slower-or-equal backend. Intercept-only does NOT suffice; delivering FlashInfer's actual value requires being inside vLLM's attention backend (framework cooperation), exactly the vLLM-source-cooperation line the team has repeatedly hit as OUT (cipher-ra-path1-build-wall: 'hosting needs vLLM SOURCE COOPERATION = OUT per substrate line').
assessment.reasoning: Sources: FlashInfer paper arXiv 2501.01005 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.01005, html v1/v2) — headline 29-69% ITL is vs Triton/compiler backend in SGLang v0.3.4; 28-30% long-context is vs FlashAttention unfused kernel (Streaming-LLM, Vicuna-13B); 13-17% parallel-gen is vs no-composable-formats ablation in MLC-Engine; experiments on A100-40GB + H100-80GB; integration is plan()/run() kernel-library API, plan stage not CUDAGraph-captured. CRITIQUES/BENCHMARKS: vLLM issue #9471 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/9471) — FlashInfer 16% SLOWER than FlashAttention on H100, Llama-3.1-8B-FP8, batch=64 (5020 vs 6003 tok/s), the exact FP8/7B/H100 case. vLLM issue #6617 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/6617) — FlashInfer 'quite marginal' for long-context Qwen2-72B-128k, closed not-planned. vLLM attention-backend docs/DeepWiki (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/attention_backends/) — H100/SM90 default is FlashAttention-3; FlashInfer is auto-fallback only on Blackwell SM100, not Hopper; backend chosen via VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND flag. WHERE IT'S REAL (not denied): skewed/variable-length batch 70-83% BW vs ~45% FA (flashinfer.ai blog + paper), H20 batch-decode beats FA3 (Dao-AILab flash-attention issue #1572), and FlashInfer 0.2 already folds FA3 templates (flashinfer.ai 2024-12-16 release). NET: gain is real but baseline-inflated (vs Triton), does not hold vs the FA3 production default on saturated batched H100 FP8 (the team's setup), and even the regime where it wins is not reachable by a GEMM-intercepting substrate without forking/wiring vLLM's attention backend — which the substrate definition forbids. The earlier research pass's 'yes-pure-substrate / model-dep none' is wrong on the substrate axis: it conflated 'no model retrain' (true) with 'driver-interposable' (false). FlashInfer needs framework-change, not interception.

assessment.technique: Machete (Hopper mixed-input W4A16 GEMM; CUTLASS 3.5.1 TMA+WGMMA, Marlin successor; ships in vLLM 0.6.2+ via PR #7174)
assessment.honest_gain: The substrate's actual setup is 7B-dense / vLLM / FP8 — and for THAT setup the honest expected gain is roughly ZERO-to-negative, not the headline +29-42%. The headline numbers are real but model-and-load-specific: +29% input / +32% output throughput on Llama-3.1-70B (1xH100) and +42% on 405B (4xH100), measured by Red Hat/Neural Magic ONLY at 3+ req/s and ONLY where Machete is the selected kernel (batch ~128+). Two facts gut the transfer to this team: (1) SCALE — the gains come from 70B/405B where the weight-stream dominates; on 8B-class models the win is far smaller. Independent SqueezeBits benchmark (Llama-3.1-8B, H100) shows W4A16 gives ~2x only at batch-1 decode (memory-bound), and the advantage 'largely compressed' to FP16 parity at batch 256 (saturated/compute-bound). A real vLLM bug report (#21266, Llama-3-8B, H100, Machete/Marlin kernel loaded) shows W4A16 at ~15% SLOWER than FP16 in a low-batch real config (1043 vs 1233 req/s) — directly corroborating this team's own 'INT4 GEMV is WORSE at batch-1' finding. (2) BASELINE — Red Hat itself states that at batch 128+ Machete is only 'competitive with FP16,' i.e. W4A16's benefit is bandwidth, which evaporates exactly in the saturated/compute-bound regime where a serving fleet operates. So for 7B-dense on vLLM, the realistic outcome is: a memory bandwidth/cost win (4x smaller weights -> larger effective batch, lower TTFT at low load) but NOT a throughput win at saturated load, and a latency LOSS at batch-1. Plus an accuracy cost: ~98.9% OpenLLM-v1 / 96.1% OpenLLM-v2 recovery for 8B W4A16 (Neural Magic eval). Net for this team: not a throughput lever, a memory-footprint/capacity lever with a small quality tax.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only does NOT suffice, and this is the fine print the research pass glossed. Machete is not a drop-in kernel swap a GOT-patcher can apply transparently: it consumes 4-bit packed weights + group scales (GPTQ/AWQ layout), not the bf16/fp16 weight tensors vLLM holds. To deliver it the substrate would have to (a) obtain or generate a W4A16 quantized checkpoint (LLM Compressor / GPTQ / AWQ) — that is MODEL COOPERATION, a new artifact loaded by vLLM, the opposite of 'runs under unmodified vLLM with no model retrain'; and (b) make vLLM dispatch its Linear layers through the Machete/compressed-tensors linear method — which in practice is vLLM's own quantization config + MacheteLinearKernel selection path, NOT something achievable by GOT-patching cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM symbols underneath an unmodified bf16 model. Intercepting cublasGemmEx and substituting a mixed-input W4A16 GEMM at the driver level is a non-starter because the caller passes fp16 A and fp16 B pointers; there are no 4-bit weights or scales in the call to dequant from. The honest substrate verdict: Machete is delivered by vLLM-the-framework when fed a quantized checkpoint, NOT by a CUDA-interposition substrate. Where the substrate CAN add value is orthogonal and modest: cross-process/cross-tenant kernel-selection telemetry, verifying Machete vs Marlin selection at the right batch boundary, and clock/power policy around it — but it cannot be the thing that turns on the W4A16 speedup.
assessment.reasoning: Primary source: Red Hat/Neural Magic 'Introducing Machete' (developers.redhat.com/articles/2024/10/14) — fetched, confirms +29%/+32% (70B 1xH100) and +42% (405B 4xH100) all gated at '3+ req/s', that Machete beats marlin/gemlite/fbgemm_i4 only at 'batch sizes 128 and above', that at batch 128+ it is merely 'competitive with FP16', and that sub-32 batch is explicitly open future work (no accuracy numbers given). In-tree reality: vLLM PR #7174 (LucasWilkinson), ships vLLM 0.6.2+. Critical independent corroboration on 7B/8B-scale (the team's actual size): SqueezeBits 'vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM #6 Weight-only Quantization' (Llama-3.1-8B, H100) — W4A16 ~2x at batch-1 memory-bound but advantage 'largely compressed' to FP16 parity at batch 256; kernel selection ExLlamaV2(b1)->Marlin(b4-16)->Machete(b64-256). Real regression evidence: vLLM issue #21266 (Llama-3-8B, H100, 'Using MacheteLinearKernel') — W4A16 ~15% SLOWER than FP16 at low batch, closed not-planned. Mechanism corroborated by multiple sources: W4A16 dequants to FP16 and computes in FP16, so it saves bandwidth not FLOPs; at large batch the workload becomes compute-bound and the win collapses (W4A16 ~10% vs W8A8 ~40% at batch 256, per weight-activation-quant analysis). Accuracy: Neural Magic eval (huggingface neuralmagic/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-quantized.w4a16) 98.9% OpenLLM-v1 / 96.1% v2 recovery; corroborated by 'We ran over half a million evaluations' (Red Hat) ~99% avg, min 96%. The research pass's 'yes-with-model-cooperation' is directionally right that it needs a quantized checkpoint, but understated TWO things: (1) it ALSO needs framework dispatch (vLLM quant config), not just a checkpoint a substrate can inject; (2) the +29-42% is a 70B/405B number that does not transfer to 7B, where independent benchmarks show parity-to-regression at the loads a fleet runs.

research.summary: Serving-system and scheduling levers are where the LARGEST measured tokens/GPU and $/token wins in modern LLM serving come from — far larger than any single-kernel optimization — but they live at the FRAMEWORK and ORCHESTRATOR layer, not at the GEMM/kernel-interception layer. Continuous batching + PagedAttention (Orca/vLLM) is the foundational unlock (up to ~23x over naive batching, 24x over HF Transformers) and is already inside any unmodified vLLM the substrate runs under. Prefill-decode disaggregation (DistServe up to 4.5-7.4x goodput; Splitwise 2.35x throughput/cost; Mooncake +59-498% effective capacity, +115% real requests; NVIDIA Dynamo ~2x-30x depending on model/HW) is the biggest system-level throughput-per-GPU lever AT SCALE, but the 2025-2026 pragmatic consensus is it only wins under high load / large fleets / long sequences with fast KV-transfer interconnect, and chunked-prefill COLOCATION (Sarathi-Serve) is better at low-to-moderate load. The single biggest $/token lever is prefix/KV-cache reuse + cache-aware routing (cuts decode-pool token cost to ~18% of monolithic in one analysis; SGLang cache-aware LB 1.9x throughput / 3.8x hit-rate). CRITICALLY: a CUDA-driver-interposition substrate that runs under unmodified vLLM and does not fork the framework or own the orchestrator CANNOT itself disaggregate, batch, page, route, or cache — those are framework/cluster decisions. Its cross-process/cross-tenant visibility is genuinely valuable as a SIGNAL SOURCE to inform a scheduler/router, but delivering these gains requires a framework or orchestrator change, not pure interception.

techniques.name: Continuous batching / iteration-level scheduling (Orca, vLLM)
techniques.mechanism: Admit and retire requests at every decode iteration instead of at fixed batch boundaries, so finished sequences free their slots immediately and waiting requests join mid-flight, keeping the GPU saturated.
techniques.reported_gain: Up to 23x throughput over naive/static batching (Anyscale benchmark); Orca 36.9x over FasterTransformer at equal latency (OSDI'22); vLLM original release 24x over HF Transformers and 3.5x over HF TGI when combined with PagedAttention.
techniques.axis: throughput (tokens/GPU)
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: n/a (already in unmodified vLLM; the substrate runs under it and cannot re-implement the scheduler from the driver layer)

techniques.name: PagedAttention KV-cache management (vLLM)
techniques.mechanism: Store KV-cache in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks (like OS paging) to nearly eliminate memory fragmentation, allowing far larger effective batch sizes for the same HBM.
techniques.reported_gain: Part of vLLM's 24x-over-HF / 3.5x-over-TGI headline; reduces KV memory waste from ~60-80% to <4% (vLLM SOSP'23). The throughput win comes from the larger batches it enables, not from compute.
techniques.axis: throughput (via larger batch / better HBM utilization)
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: n/a (lives inside vLLM's attention + memory manager; a GEMM-interception substrate does not own the KV allocator)

techniques.name: Chunked prefill + decode piggybacking (SARATHI / Sarathi-Serve)
techniques.mechanism: Split a long prefill into equal chunks and fill the rest of each batch with decode tokens ('decode-maximal' / stall-free batching), so the compute-heavy prefill subsidizes the memory-bound decodes in the same iteration and avoids decode stalls.
techniques.reported_gain: LLaMA-13B/A6000: up to 10x decode throughput, 1.33x end-to-end; LLaMA-33B/A100: 1.25x e2e, 4.25x decode; GPT-3 with pipeline parallelism: 6.29x fewer bubbles -> 1.91x e2e (SARATHI arXiv 2308.16369). Sarathi-Serve is the production default 'colocation' alternative to disaggregation.
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (tames throughput-latency tradeoff)
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: n/a as substrate (it is a scheduler policy inside vLLM/Sarathi; the substrate cannot reshape batches at the driver layer)

techniques.name: Prefill-decode disaggregation (DistServe)
techniques.mechanism: Run prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) on separate GPU pools so they stop interfering; pick parallelism/placement per pool via simulator search to maximize per-GPU goodput under dual TTFT/TPOT SLOs; KV-cache is transferred prefill->decode.
techniques.reported_gain: Up to 4.48x goodput or 10.2x tighter SLO vs SOTA (paper headline 'up to 7.4x more goodput or 12.6x stricter SLO' while keeping >90% requests in budget), OSDI'24, arXiv 2401.09670.
techniques.axis: goodput (throughput under SLO) per GPU
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: weeks-months at orchestrator level (needs separate pools, KV transfer, SLO-aware router) — out of reach for a single-process under-vLLM substrate; substrate can only supply cross-tenant load signal to such a router

techniques.name: Disaggregation with heterogeneous hardware (Splitwise)
techniques.mechanism: Put compute-bound prefill on high-FLOP GPUs (H100) and memory-bound decode on cheaper/older high-bandwidth GPUs (A100), matching each phase to the cheapest hardware that fits its bottleneck.
techniques.reported_gain: 2.35x more throughput under the same power+cost budget, or 1.4x higher throughput at 20% lower cost (Splitwise, Patel et al., ISCA'24).
techniques.axis: throughput-per-dollar / throughput-per-watt
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: months (cross-hardware fleet design + KV transfer); substrate-irrelevant to the routing decision itself

techniques.name: KVCache-centric disaggregation + global cache pool (Mooncake)
techniques.mechanism: Disaggregate prefill/decode clusters AND build a global KV-cache pool across underused CPU/DRAM/SSD of the cluster, with a cache- and SLO-aware scheduler; trades cheap storage for expensive recomputation, especially for long shared contexts.
techniques.reported_gain: +59% to +498% effective request capacity on real traces under SLO; up to +525% throughput in simulation; in production Kimi serves +115% (A800) and +107% (H800) more requests (Mooncake, FAST'25 / arXiv 2407.00079).
techniques.axis: throughput / effective request capacity per GPU under SLO
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: months (global cache tier + scheduler); the cross-process KV visibility a substrate has is conceptually aligned but it does not own vLLM's KV blocks

techniques.name: Production disaggregated serving stack (NVIDIA Dynamo)
techniques.mechanism: Orchestrator that does disaggregated prefill/decode with NIXL KV transfer, KV-aware routing, and SLO-based autoscaling across multi-node fleets, on top of vLLM/TensorRT-LLM/SGLang backends.
techniques.reported_gain: ~2x throughput on Llama-70B/Hopper; up to 30x more requests / 2.5x tokens/s/GPU on DeepSeek-R1/GB200 NVL72; up to 7x on DeepSeek-R1/Blackwell; Dynamo 0.4 'up to 4x' generationally (NVIDIA blogs, 2025-2026). Community: 2.2k tok/s/H200 sustained multi-node (vLLM wide-EP).
techniques.axis: throughput (tokens/GPU) at fleet scale
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: months (this IS the orchestrator the substrate would have to either become or feed); confirms the lever lives above the driver layer

techniques.name: Automatic prefix caching (APC, vLLM)
techniques.mechanism: Hash and reuse KV blocks for shared prefixes (system prompts, few-shot, multi-turn) so repeated prefills are skipped; speeds up the prefill phase / TTFT for cache hits.
techniques.reported_gain: Modest in-instance: ~13.3% throughput / ~9.8% TPOT improvement (SqueezeBits vLLM-vs-TRT-LLM); in high-reuse shared-prefix workloads, +254% output token throughput (427->1513 tok/s) and -78% TTFT (4.3s->under 1s). Hurts slightly when hit-rate is near zero (hashing overhead).
techniques.axis: throughput + latency (TTFT), workload-dependent
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: n/a (built into vLLM; gated on the framework owning the KV cache, not the GEMM stream)

techniques.name: Cache-aware / prefix-aware request routing (SGLang LB, llm-d)
techniques.mechanism: A router maintains an approximate view of each worker's KV/prefix cache (radix tree or introspected vLLM cache) and routes each request to the worker most likely to have its prefix cached, maximizing hit-rate and balancing load.
techniques.reported_gain: SGLang v0.4 cache-aware LB: up to 1.9x throughput and 3.8x cache hit-rate; llm-d prefix+load-aware scheduling reduces tail latency and raises throughput on 16xH100 enterprise B2B workload (numbers qualitative in the post).
techniques.axis: throughput + TTFT + $/token (via hit-rate)
techniques.model_dependency: none model-side, but needs cooperation from the router/orchestrator and read-access to per-worker cache state
techniques.impl_cost: weeks IF the substrate is allowed to act as / feed the router — this is the ONE place a cross-process, cross-tenant substrate signal is genuinely differentiating (it already sees all tenants), but actuating the routing decision still requires an orchestrator hook, not pure interception

techniques.name: Multi-LoRA serving (S-LoRA, Punica)
techniques.mechanism: Serve thousands of LoRA adapters over one shared base model using batched heterogeneous-adapter GEMM kernels (SGMV/BGMV) + unified paging of adapter+KV memory, so many fine-tunes share one weight stream.
techniques.reported_gain: Punica 12x throughput vs vLLM and near-constant latency vs adapter count; S-LoRA up to 4x vs vLLM (few adapters) and 30x vs PEFT, serving 2000 adapters concurrently (S-LoRA arXiv 2311.03285, Punica MLSys'24).
techniques.axis: throughput / cost (many tenants per GPU)
techniques.model_dependency: trained LoRA adapters (per tenant), plus framework support for the batched-adapter kernels
techniques.impl_cost: n/a as pure substrate (needs custom adapter kernels + the serving framework's batching path; not reachable by intercepting base-model GEMMs)

techniques.name: Speculative decoding combined with disaggregation (EAGLE-3)
techniques.mechanism: A small draft model/head proposes multiple tokens that the base model verifies in one forward pass, turning memory-bound serial decode into a more parallel verify; pairs naturally with disaggregation since draft+verify stress different resources.
techniques.reported_gain: EAGLE-3: 3-4x decode throughput at small batch on H100/H200 (acceptance 0.80-0.88); SGLang single-H100: 1.81x at batch 2, still 1.38x at batch 64; Medusa/EAGLE ~2.4-2.8x on A100. Gains shrink as batch grows (compute saturates).
techniques.axis: latency + throughput (mainly small/medium batch decode)
techniques.model_dependency: trained draft model or EAGLE/Medusa heads tied to the base model
techniques.impl_cost: n/a as substrate (requires trained heads + verify-loop integration in the framework; the substrate cannot synthesize a draft model by interception)

techniques.name: Disaggregation crossover / when colocation wins (pragmatic 2025-2026 take)
techniques.mechanism: Empirical finding that disaggregation only beats chunked-prefill colocation under high load, large batches, long sequences, and large fleets with fast KV-transfer interconnect; at low-to-moderate load the KV-transfer + sync overhead makes colocation (Sarathi-Serve) cheaper. This bounds the realistic gain of any disaggregation play.

Optimized NCCL KV pipelines cut transfer latency 96.8-98.2% vs naive, which is what makes the win possible.

techniques.model_dependency: none — the substrate's cross-tenant load/utilization view is exactly the signal needed to decide WHEN to disaggregate, but it must feed an orchestrator that owns placement and KV transfer
techniques.impl_cost: the actuation is months (orchestrator); the SIGNAL (cross-process load, per-GPU memory pressure, prefix overlap across tenants) is where a substrate adds unique value cheaply (days-weeks) if a router will consume it

assessment.technique: Cache-aware / prefix-aware request routing (SGLang cache-aware LB, llm-d precise prefix-cache scheduling, vLLM production-stack / Ray PrefixCacheAffinityRouter)
assessment.honest_gain:
For THIS team's defined product (a single-GPU CUDA-driver-interposition substrate running under one unmodified vLLM): ~0x. Routing is a decision made ACROSS multiple replicas; with one vLLM instance there is no route to choose, and vLLM v1's built-in Automatic Prefix Caching already captures the entire within-replica prefix-reuse win for free. The substrate gains nothing it doesn't already get.

The published gains are real but apply to a MULTI-REPLICA FLEET, not a single GPU, and they are highly workload-dependent (only materialize on shared-prefix / multi-turn / agentic / multi-tenant B2B traffic with repeating high-cardinality prefixes):
- SGLang v0.4 cache-aware LB: 1.9x throughput, 3.8x cache hit-rate (20% to 75%), 82,665 to 158,596 tok/s — but on 8x A100-80GB workers, Llama-3.1-8B, vs NAIVE round-robin, on a SYNTHETIC 'multiple long prefix groups, perfectly balanced' workload. LMSYS explicitly caveats 'performance might vary based on the characteristics of the workload.' Not H100, not 7B-on-one-GPU, not a saturated mixed trace.
- llm-d precise prefix-cache scheduling: +159.5% req/s, +159.8% output tok/s, mean TTFT -99.5% (13.3s to 0.30s), P90 TTFT 31s to 0.54s, E2E latency -39.9% — but on 16x H100 (8 pods x 2 GPU), Qwen-32B, a multi-tenant workload of 150 enterprise customers each with a 6,000-token shared prefix driving cache demand to 73% of cluster capacity (6x a single pod), vs random scheduling. The huge TTFT numbers are an artifact of comparing against a baseline that thrashes cache at 60 QPS; against vLLM's own APC + a basic load balancer the delta is far smaller.
Honest expected lift if this team built a fleet router on top of N>=2 H100/7B vLLM replicas with genuinely repeating prefixes: order ~1.3-1.9x throughput and large TTFT reductions are plausible — but that is a NEW orchestration product, not a substrate feature, and the gain collapses toward 0 on low-prefix-reuse traffic and on a single replica.
assessment.substrate_reality:
The substrate as DEFINED (intercepts cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM + CUDA kernels via GOT-patching at the driver level, single-process/single-GPU view, runs under unmodified vLLM, no vLLM fork, no model retrain) CANNOT deliver this. Prefix-aware routing lives one or two layers ABOVE where CIPHER operates:
- Physically it is an external router/gateway in front of MULTIPLE vLLM replicas: SGLang's data-parallel router (approximate radix tree mirroring workers), llm-d's Inference Gateway = Envoy ext_proc + Endpoint Picker scoring pods, vLLM production-stack vllm-router-service, or Ray PrefixCacheAffinityRouter. CIPHER intercepts GPU calls inside ONE process; it has no request-admission point and no view of sibling replicas' caches.
- The cache-state signal is an HTTP/gRPC/ZMQ control-plane artifact, not a CUDA call. llm-d consumes a stream of KVEvents emitted by vLLM over a ZMQ socket (--kv-events-config, block-hash via sha256_cbor_64bit) into kvevents.Pool -> kvcache.Index; SGLang maintains its own approximate radix tree from request metadata. None of this crosses the CUDA driver boundary CIPHER patches. The cross-process visibility CIPHER claims is same-host GPU-context visibility (NVML/ioctl), NOT a fleet-wide token-prefix-to-pod index across nodes.
- 'Intercept-only' is therefore insufficient by a wide margin. To deliver this the team would have to BUILD a separate multi-replica request router/scheduler (a distinct orchestration service), which the product definition explicitly excludes ('runs UNDER an unmodified vLLM,' single-substrate). It is not a CUDA-interposition technique at all. The research pass's 'yes-with-model-cooperation' is mis-scoped: model cooperation is irrelevant; what's needed is a FRAMEWORK/ORCHESTRATOR layer (a new router process consuming vLLM's KVEvents) the substrate does not and cannot be.
- Even the single-replica fallback is already taken: vLLM v1 Automatic Prefix Caching does hash-based block reuse automatically. CIPHER cannot improve on it without forking vLLM's scheduler/KV manager, which is out of bounds.
assessment.reasoning: SGLang numbers and conditions from the LMSYS v0.4 blog (cache-aware LB: 1.9x throughput / 3.8x hit-rate, 82,665->158,596 tok/s, 20%->75% hit-rate, 8x A100-80GB, Llama-3.1-8B, vs naive round-robin, synthetic 'multiple long prefix groups perfectly balanced' workload, with explicit 'performance might vary' caveat) — https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-12-04-sglang-v0-4/. llm-d precise prefix-cache scheduling numbers and architecture (output tok/s 8730 precise vs 6944 approximate vs 4429 load-aware; mean TTFT 0.298s vs 13.3s; P90 TTFT 0.542s vs 31s/94.9s; +159.5%/+159.8% throughput, TTFT -99.5%, E2E -39.9%; 16x H100 / 8 pods x 2 GPU; Qwen-32B; 150-customer multi-tenant B2B with 6,000-token shared prefixes at 73% cluster cache capacity; cache state via KVEvents stream over ZMQ into kvevents.Pool + kvcache.Index) — https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see and Red Hat Developer 'Master KV cache aware routing with llm-d.' Architecture (external gateway in front of multiple vLLM instances, Envoy ext_proc + Endpoint Picker, --kv-events-config ZMQ, sha256_cbor_64bit block hashes; requires >=2 replicas) from vLLM production-stack prefix-aware-routing docs and the KV-Cache Interoperability RFC #20492. Single-replica/low-cardinality fallback behavior and workload-dependence from Ray PrefixCacheAffinityRouter docs (>=10% match routes to highest-prefix replica, <10% falls back to power-of-two-choices, no prefix data = default LB) — confirming the gain is conditional on multi-replica + high-cardinality repeating prefixes, and that single-replica reuse is already handled by vLLM's built-in Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM v1 docs). Net: gains are real and reproducible BUT (1) measured on multi-GPU fleets vs weak baselines on prefix-heavy/synthetic workloads, (2) hold in production only for shared-prefix-heavy traffic (agentic/multi-turn/multi-tenant), collapsing on diverse traffic, and (3) live in an orchestration/gateway layer the single-GPU CUDA-interposition substrate is architecturally not part of. Verdict: not-for-this-setup (it would be a separate fleet-router product, not a substrate feature).

assessment.technique: Speculative decoding + disaggregation (EAGLE-3 / EAGLE-3.1 / Medusa-class draft heads)
assessment.honest_gain: Real but batch-dependent and NOT pure-substrate. The headline "3-4x" is a single-user / batch-1-2 memory-bound number; it decays hard under production concurrency. Vendor-reported (vLLM/SGLang) single-H100 EAGLE-3: ~1.81x @ batch 2, falling to ~1.38x @ batch 64; on B200, EAGLE-3 measured at only 1.05-1.23x @ concurrency 64 (P-EAGLE blog). Acceptance length ~3 tokens (acceptance rate 0.80-0.88 on coding/instruct, lower on diverse traffic). For THIS team's stated setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8, SATURATED batched serving): honest expected gain is roughly 1.2-1.5x decode throughput at low-to-moderate concurrency and approaching ~1.0x (and historically BELOW 1.0x in older vLLM/SGLang integrations) once batch >~32 makes verification compute-bound — which is exactly the regime the substrate already proved (>batch-32 the GPU is compute-bound, spec decode should be disabled). And this gain is unreachable WITHOUT a trained per-model draft head and vLLM-internal scheduler/runner integration, so for an intercept-only substrate the deliverable gain is ~0. The "no-needs-model-training" claim in the research pass is FALSE: the EAGLE-3 head is a trained artifact, per-base-model, tokenizer-locked.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only does NOT suffice — this is the decisive finding. Speculative decoding is not a GEMM/cuBLAS/cutlass call or a CUDA kernel that GOT-patching can intercept and substitute. It is a control-flow + scheduling change living inside vLLM's EagleProposer, scheduler, and model-runner: (a) run a draft head to propose K tokens, (b) build a chain/tree of candidates, (c) batch them into ONE verify forward pass of the base model with custom position-ids and attention masks, (d) sample/accept-reject, (e) ROLL BACK KV-cache slot allocations for rejected tokens (a host-side post-processing step the scheduler must own). The "Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" paper (arXiv 2510.22876) shows the hard part is precisely the ragged-tensor/KV-cache/position-id surgery across a continuous batch — realignment is ~40% of compute and naive implementations corrupt outputs (0-2% exact-match vs autoregressive). A GOT-level interposition substrate sees individual GEMM/kernel calls AFTER the framework has already decided what to run; it cannot inject a draft model, cannot restructure the batch into a verify step, cannot allocate/rollback paged-KV slots, and cannot author the variable-length accept logic. Delivering EAGLE-3 requires (1) forking/patching vLLM (EagleProposer + scheduler are already upstream, so really it means USING vLLM's native flag, not the substrate) and (2) shipping a trained, base-model-specific draft checkpoint (per-model, tokenizer-matched, multi-GPU training + TBs of hidden-state cache to produce). Both violate the substrate's stated constraints (intercept-only, no model retrain, no vLLM fork). The "disaggregation" pairing is likewise an orchestrator/serving-topology decision, not something driver interposition controls. Net: substrate would have to build essentially a whole speculative serving stack it is architecturally not positioned to build; the right home for this feature is vLLM's own spec-decode config, not CIPHER.
assessment.reasoning: Sources and what each established: (1) vLLM blog "EAGLE 3.1" (vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-26-eagle-3-1) — measured 2.03x@C=1, 1.71x@C=4, 1.66x@C=16 on GB200 (NOT H100), showing decay with concurrency; draft head trained+open-sourced per base model. (2) vLLM blog "P-EAGLE" (vllm.ai/blog/2026-03-13-p-eagle) — EAGLE-3 on B200 drops to 1.05-1.23x at concurrency 64; P-EAGLE needs `parallel_drafting:true` + specially-trained drafter heads = framework + model change. (3) "Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" (arXiv 2510.22876, A100) — ALL existing batch spec-decode impls violate output equivalence (DSD 0% exact-match, BSP 1.9%->0.2%), root cause is ragged-tensor/KV/position-id desync; realignment ~40% of compute; explicitly notes vLLM spec decode underperformed baseline at high concurrency and SGLang+EAGLE shows negative speedups across batch sizes. (4) Original EAGLE-3 paper (arXiv 2503.01840) + SGLang numbers reported via search — 1.81x@batch2, 1.38x@batch64 single-H100, EAGLE-2 regressed to 0.93x@batch24. (5) vLLM docs (docs.vllm.ai spec_decode + speculators/eagle3) — method must be eagle3, draft runs draft_tensor_parallel_size=1, EAGLE head reuses base-model layer features and is trained to match base logits = tightly model-coupled; implemented as EagleProposer inside the model runner. (6) HF/SGLang/NVIDIA EAGLE-3 checkpoints — per-base-model (Llama-3.3-70B etc.), tokenizer must match exactly or acceptance collapses; training needs 4-8 GPUs + 2-5 TB hidden-state cache. (7) Multiple practitioner sources (premai, rajatpandit, bentoml) — spec decode is a batch-1 memory-bound win, becomes counterproductive and "should be disabled" above batch ~32 when the GPU is compute-bound, consistent with the team's own established >batch-32 compute-bound finding. It is genuinely valuable in production — but as a vLLM-native feature the customer enables, not as a CIPHER substrate deliverable.

assessment.technique: Disaggregation crossover / when colocation wins (pragmatic 2025-2026 take): the empirical finding that prefill/decode disaggregation only beats chunked-prefill colocation (Sarathi-Serve style) under high load + large batches + long/prefill-heavy sequences + large fleets with fast KV-transfer interconnect; at low-to-moderate load the KV-transfer + scheduling/sync overhead makes colocation cheaper.
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, single-to-moderate-fleet vLLM, FP8), the honest expected gain from a disaggregation PLAY is ~0, and likely negative at low load. The crossover THESIS is real and well-supported, but it points AGAINST disaggregation here: (a) Beyond the Buzz (arXiv 2506.05508) finds disaggregation wins for prefill-heavy (ISL>>OSL) and models >10B; a 7B model is below its model-size sweet spot and decode-heavy chat traffic is exactly where they say co-located piggybacking (chunked prefill) wins. (b) DuetServe (arXiv 2511.04791, H100+NVLink, Qwen3-8B/14B) measured aggregated vLLM saturating at QPS=7 with HIGHER total throughput (~5.0 vs ~3.5 req/s) than disaggregated Dynamo, and disagg-Dynamo delivering 'less than half the total tokens/s' of agg-vLLM on 8B — disaggregation only won on TBT/latency stability, not throughput or cost. So at 7B on H100, chunked-prefill colocation (already vLLM's default) is the throughput/cost winner; the substrate cannot beat the framework default it already runs under. Where a real disaggregation gain exists at all, it is at large scale: Splitwise's verifiable number is 1.4x throughput at 20% lower hardware cost (decode-heavy: 2.35x under same power), and DistServe's is up to 7.4x / 4.48x GOODPUT (not cost) — both at multi-replica scale with fast interconnect, not a single-node 7B deployment. The 'token cost ~18% of monolithic at 4x (not 7x)' figure could NOT be verified in either Beyond the Buzz or the Momento routing blog as fetched; treat it as an unsourced/synthesized number — do NOT cite it as a product target.
assessment.substrate_reality: The substrate canNOT deliver disaggregation intercept-only. Production vLLM disaggregation (verified against vLLM docs, NVIDIA Dynamo docs, LMCache) requires: (1) a KVConnector implementation (KVConnectorBase_V1 / NixlConnector) that moves KV blocks VRAM-to-VRAM over RDMA/NVLink — this is in-engine code, not a GOT-patchable cuBLAS/kernel call; (2) a proxy/PrefillRouter that OWNS request placement and routes prompt->prefiller then forwards KV metadata->decoder; (3) separate prefill/decode worker pools with fast interconnect (NIXL over NVLink/InfiniBand). A driver-interposition substrate that GOT-patches GEMM/kernel calls and sets clocks sees none of the placement/KV-movement plane and cannot author it without forking vLLM or shipping a connector — both explicitly out of the substrate's definition (no vLLM fork, intercept-only). The ONE genuinely true part of the deliverability claim: the substrate's cross-process/cross-tenant load+utilization view IS exactly the right SIGNAL to decide WHEN load justifies disaggregation (the crossover decision the literature says is the hard part). But that makes the substrate a sensor/advisor feeding an external orchestrator that owns placement and KV transfer — NOT a delivery mechanism. Intercept-only is insufficient; this is needs-framework-change / needs-orchestrator. FlowKV's 96.8%/98.2% NCCL-transfer-latency reductions are real but are transfer-latency-only on simulated data (A100/L20, 8B) and only matter AFTER you have already built the disaggregated topology — they do not create a win for a single-node 7B vLLM and are not something the substrate produces.
assessment.reasoning: Sources, with what each actually supports/refutes: (1) Beyond the Buzz: A Pragmatic Take on Inference Disaggregation, arXiv 2506.05508 — CONFIRMS the directional thesis (disaggregation wins for prefill-heavy ISL>>OSL and models >10B; co-located piggybacking wins decode-heavy) but explicitly assumes 'sufficient GPUs and incoming requests to fully utilize the rate-matched deployment,' i.e. it SIDESTEPS the low-load regime the technique claims, and does NOT contain the 18%/4x/7x cost numbers. (2) DuetServe, arXiv 2511.04791 — DECISIVE production rebuttal on the exact target hardware class: H100+NVLink, Qwen3-8B/14B, 8K input/200 output; Figure 2 shows aggregated vLLM saturates at QPS=7 with higher total throughput than disaggregated Dynamo, disagg only stabilizes TBT, and 'Disagg-Dynamo achieves less than half the total tokens per second of Agg-vLLM' due to single-GPU prefill bottleneck. (3) Momento 'Disaggregated Inference Part 1' blog — gives the practical crossover heuristics (KV transfer adds 50-200ms; ~250ms TTFT for Llama-70B; 'disaggregation only wins if that beats the tail latency you're already eating'; right strategy 'isn't universal') and the verifiable Splitwise number (1.4x throughput / 20% lower hardware cost; 2.35x at same power, decode-heavy) — but did NOT contain the 18% claim. (4) Spheron/GenAI-system-design 2026 guides — corroborate colocation-wins regimes: <10 concurrent users, <512-token prompts, latency-sensitive single-model deployments, PCIe-only links. (5) FlowKV, arXiv 2504.03775 — 96.8% (vs vLLM-Disagg) and 98.2% (vs Mooncake RDMA) avg KV-transfer-latency reduction, but Section 4.4 notes these are on 'simulated data,' A100/L20/H20, Llama-3.1-8B/70B, no H100, and the paper acknowledges no failure modes (advocacy framing). (6) vLLM docs (NixlConnector usage), NVIDIA Dynamo disaggregated-serving docs, LMCache NIXL blog — establish that disaggregation requires an in-engine KVConnector + external proxy/PrefillRouter owning placement, which an intercept-only substrate cannot author. (7) DistServe + Hao AI Lab 18-months-later retro — source of the 4.48x/7.4x GOODPUT (not cost) numbers; the retro is advocacy ('default playbook for large-scale serving') and conspicuously omits any 7B / small-fleet defense, consistent with disaggregation being a large-scale play. Net: the crossover thesis is real and supersedes naive 7x-cost disaggregation hype, but for H100/7B/vLLM/FP8 it argues for staying on chunked-prefill colocation; the substrate can at best be the cross-tenant load SENSOR feeding an orchestrator's disaggregation decision, not a deliverer of the gain.

research.summary: The ReLU-era contextual-sparsity win (PowerInfer/DejaVu) does NOT transfer to modern SwiGLU/SiLU models, which only show ~50% natural activation sparsity vs ~90%+ for ReLU — this is confirmed across the literature. Two training-free methods, TEAL and CATS, DO recover usable magnitude/threshold sparsity on SwiGLU models (Llama-2/3, Mistral) and deliver real measured gains, but only in batch-1 memory-bound decode: TEAL ~1.5x at 40% sparsity (near-lossless) up to ~1.8x at 50% (with ~7% PPL hit); CATS ~18-21% end-to-end. Both are pure memory-bandwidth (MBU) plays consistent with the team's batch-1 decode finding and require a custom sparse-GEMV kernel — exactly the kind of artifact a GOT-patching substrate could supply WITHOUT retraining. The fatal caveat is "union sparsity collapse": all neuron-level activation sparsity degrades toward zero gain as serving batch size grows (Polar Sparsity, DejaVu), so these are single-stream/low-batch levers, not throughput-serving levers. ReLUfication (ProSparse, 89% sparsity, up to 4.5x with PowerInfer) and predictor-based methods (Polar Sparsity, ShadowLLM) need model fine-tuning or trained routers and so fall outside a no-retraining substrate; MoE expert-offloading gains are large but apply only to MoE checkpoints, not dense 7B.

techniques.name: TEAL (training-free magnitude activation sparsity)
techniques.mechanism: Magnitude-prunes the smallest-|x| entries of every hidden-state vector feeding each linear (using offline-estimated per-tensor thresholds), then runs a sparse GEMV that only loads the weight columns/rows corresponding to surviving activations. Works on SwiGLU because it sparsifies ALL hidden states, not just the gate-activation output.
techniques.reported_gain: 1.53x wall-clock single-batch decode at 40% model-wide sparsity (PPL 5.22 vs 5.07 baseline, ~0.3% degradation) and 1.78x at 50% (PPL 5.43, ~7% degradation) on Llama-2-7B, A6000 GPU; on A100 with torch.compile baseline only 1.25-1.40x. Validated on Mistral-7B, Llama-2 7B/13B/70B, Llama-3 8B/70B (TEAL paper, arXiv 2408.14690, ICLR 2025).
techniques.axis: MBU (memory-bandwidth-bound batch-1 decode); does NOT touch compute MFU
techniques.model_dependency: none (training-free; thresholds calibrated offline from generic text). Substrate must intercept the linear GEMV calls and substitute a fused mask+sparse-GEMV kernel; no checkpoint change.
techniques.impl_cost: weeks (need a Triton/CUDA fused-threshold sparse-GEMV kernel matching the DejaVu/TEAL design, plus interception/calibration); the kernel is the hard part, not the policy

techniques.name: CATS (contextually-aware thresholding for sparsity)
techniques.mechanism: Targets the gated-MLP: computes W_gate densely, applies a learned/calibrated threshold to the SiLU gate output to zero ~50% of intermediate neurons, then skips the corresponding columns of W_up and rows of W_down via a custom sparse kernel. Training-free at zero-shot; fine-tuning recovers quality further.
techniques.reported_gain: ~18% (Llama-2-7B) and ~21% (Mistral-7B) end-to-end token-generation throughput at 50% sparsity; MLP-block latency cut ~40% at 50% / ~70% at 70% sparsity. Zero-shot accuracy cost ~1.5% (Mistral) / ~2.4% (Llama-2) average over downstream tasks at 50%; closes to comparable with 500 fine-tuning steps (CATS paper, arXiv 2404.08763).
techniques.axis: MBU (memory-bandwidth, batch-1/low-batch decode); MLP-block bandwidth only
techniques.model_dependency: none for zero-shot 50% (training-free); optional fine-tuning improves quality. Substrate intercepts the down_proj/up_proj GEMVs and supplies the gather-based sparse kernel; thresholds calibrated offline. Quality cost (1.5-2.4%) is the price of staying training-free.
techniques.impl_cost: weeks (custom MLP gather-GEMV kernel + threshold calibration; narrower scope than TEAL since MLP-only)

techniques.name: PowerInfer / DejaVu contextual sparsity (ReLU-era) — confirmed NOT applicable to SwiGLU
techniques.mechanism: Predicts which MLP neurons / attention heads are active per token with a small MLP predictor, computes only the 'hot' fraction, and (PowerInfer) keeps hot neurons GPU-resident while streaming cold ones from CPU. Relies on the >90% natural activation sparsity of ReLU/ReGLU models.
techniques.reported_gain: PowerInfer: up to ~11x on consumer GPU for ReLU models (ReluLLaMA); DejaVu ~2x on OPT. BUT on SiLU/SwiGLU models natural sparsity is only ~50%, and substituting ReGLU only reaches ~70% — too low to amortize predictor + gather overhead, so the speedup largely evaporates. This confirms the team's prior finding that contextual sparsity is a ReLU-era win (PowerInfer arXiv 2312.12456; Turbo Sparse arXiv 2406.05955).
techniques.axis: MBU (would-be), but net gain ~0 on modern SwiGLU at serving
techniques.model_dependency: needs a ReLU/ReGLU checkpoint (ReLUfication) AND trained per-layer predictors; neither exists for stock SwiGLU and both require training. A substrate cannot manufacture the sparsity that the SwiGLU activation does not have.
techniques.impl_cost: N/A for substrate (blocked: requires retrained model + predictors)

techniques.name: ProSparse / ReLUfication (activation-sparsity recovery via fine-tuning)
techniques.mechanism: Replaces SiLU/SwiGLU with ReLU and applies progressive sparsity regularization + fine-tuning to push activation sparsity to ~89% while preserving accuracy, restoring the ReLU-era contextual-sparsity regime so PowerInfer-style serving works.
techniques.reported_gain: 89.32% sparsity on Llama-2-7B, 88.80% on Llama-2-13B with accuracy comparable to the Swish original; up to 4.52x inference speedup (custom sparse kernels) / 4.65x with PowerInfer (ProSparse, arXiv 2402.13516, COLING 2025).
techniques.axis: MBU (huge, because sparsity is ~89%)
techniques.model_dependency: needs full ReLUfication + sparsity-regularized fine-tuning to produce a new checkpoint (SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b on HF). Out of bounds for a no-retraining substrate — but note: if the customer ships a ProSparse checkpoint, the substrate could then host the sparse-GEMV serving kernel (yes-with-model-cooperation in that narrow case).
techniques.impl_cost: N/A for substrate as a no-retrain product (model training is the blocker)

techniques.name: Polar Sparsity (batch-scalable contextual sparsity) — diagnoses the union-sparsity wall
techniques.mechanism: Empirically shows MLP neuron union-sparsity collapses with batch (any neuron firing for any sequence must be loaded), while attention HEAD sparsity is batch-invariant. Shifts the sparsity target from MLP to attention heads at scale using trained routers + sparsity-aware MLP and attention kernels.
techniques.reported_gain: Up to 2.2x decode throughput (OPT-66B, batch 64) and up to ~1.85x for Llama-2-7B at scale vs dense, ~2x over DejaVu, accuracy within ~1% (Polar Sparsity, arXiv 2505.14884, NeurIPS 2025). Crucially documents that plain MLP activation sparsity (TEAL/CATS/DejaVu) gives gains mainly at batch 1 and degrades sharply by batch 4+.
techniques.axis: MBU/throughput at moderate batch (its value is the batch-invariant attention-head sparsity)
techniques.model_dependency: needs trained attention/MLP routers (2-layer FFNs trained on WikiText-2 with ground-truth activation labels). A substrate cannot synthesize these routers without a training step; this is the method that would beat the batch-collapse, and it is exactly the one that needs training.
techniques.impl_cost: N/A for pure substrate (router training required); kernels themselves are buildable in weeks if routers were provided

techniques.name: LayerSkip / early-exit self-speculative decoding
techniques.mechanism: Exit at an early layer to draft tokens, then verify/correct with the remaining layers (self-speculation) — the draft and verifier share weights and KV cache, so no separate draft model. Requires the model to be trained/finetuned with layer-dropout + early-exit loss to make early layers predictive.
techniques.reported_gain: Up to 2.16x on CNN/DM summarization, 1.82x on coding, 2.0x on TOPv2 semantic parsing, across Llama sizes (LayerSkip, arXiv 2404.16710, ACL 2024). Gains are task-dependent and require the LayerSkip-trained checkpoints.
techniques.axis: latency / throughput (fewer effective layers per accepted token)
techniques.model_dependency: needs a LayerSkip-trained/continually-pretrained checkpoint with early-exit heads; stock Llama/Mistral early layers are not exit-calibrated. A substrate cannot add this without training. (Generic self-speculation without training exists but yields far smaller, unreliable gains.)
techniques.impl_cost: N/A for pure substrate (training the early-exit behavior is the blocker)

techniques.name: MoE expert offloading / sparsity-aware expert cache
techniques.mechanism: Keep full expert set in host/CPU memory, prefetch only the experts a router selects per token into GPU, exploiting the high reuse (power-law) of a few hot experts to overlap fetch with compute. Lets a single GPU serve models far larger than VRAM.
techniques.reported_gain: MoE-Infinity 3.1-16.7x lower per-token latency vs vLLM/DeepSpeed/Ollama on Mixtral & DeepSeek; MoE-Gen 16-33x higher decode throughput vs model-offloading baselines on a single GPU (arXiv 2401.14361, 2503.09716).
techniques.axis: throughput / latency / effective capacity (memory-capacity, via offload+prefetch overlap)
techniques.model_dependency: applies ONLY to MoE checkpoints (Mixtral, DeepSeek, Llama-4), NOT the dense Mistral/Llama-7B the team targets. Even for MoE, capturing the router decision and orchestrating CPU<->GPU expert prefetch needs scheduler/weight-residency control that lives in the serving framework, not purely at the GEMM-interception layer. Substrate could assist (cross-process expert-cache view) but cannot own the data path.
techniques.impl_cost: N/A for the dense-7B product; months if pivoting to MoE serving

techniques.name: Low-rank / Koopman-style GEMM surrogate (team-internal prior, cross-checked)
techniques.mechanism: Replace the FP16 GEMM Y=XW with a rank-r factored / EDMD map of activations to cut FLOPs and bytes. Distinct from activation sparsity: targets the weight-stream rank rather than activation support.
techniques.reported_gain: No external paper supports a usable lossless gain on 7B SwiGLU at the ranks needed; activation effective rank of Llama lm_head is ~844 (90%) / ~2630 (99%) of 4096, so r=64 is ~13-40x too small — the team's own measurement (cipher-koopman-rank-frontier) found the rank-64 kernel ~20-25x slower than cuBLAS and it never fires the OOD gate (residual ~0.96 vs 0.05). No verifiable speedup.
techniques.axis: would-be MFU/MBU, but no realizable lossless operating point found
techniques.model_dependency: a faithful low-rank map needs per-layer fitting (effectively training) and still fails the OOD/quality gate at FLOP-saving ranks; substrate-hostable in principle but there is no accurate-and-fast operating point to host.
techniques.impl_cost: already explored and walled by the team; not a near-term product lever

assessment.technique: TEAL (training-free magnitude activation sparsity, arXiv 2408.14690, ICLR 2025)
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8, production/batched serving) the honest expected gain is ~1.0x — essentially nothing. Three independent reasons, all from the primary sources: (1) BATCH COLLAPSE. The win is a batch-1, memory-bound-decode phenomenon. The TEAL paper itself shows W_down sparsity falling from ~60% to ~38% at batch=4 for equal error; the NeurIPS 2025 follow-up Polar Sparsity quantifies that the *union* of active neurons across a batch grows toward dense as batch size rises, so 'union neuron sparsity diminishes with batching' and MLP sparsity 'breaks down under batched workloads.' vLLM continuous batching saturates exactly this regime, so the weight-stream reduction TEAL relies on evaporates. (2) HARDWARE/BASELINE DERATING. Headline 1.53x/1.78x is A6000 at 40%/50% sparsity. On A100 (closest public proxy to H100) it is only 1.25-1.34x (40%) and 1.33-1.45x (50%) against a torch.compile/gpt-fast baseline — and H100's higher HBM bandwidth + better tensor-core utilization shrinks the memory-bound headroom further, so expect the bottom of that range or less even at batch-1. (3) QUALITY/PRECISION. The cited PPL is the 40% point (5.22 vs 5.07, ~0.3%); pushing to 50% for the bigger 1.78x costs ~7% PPL, which fails a serving quality bar. And the kernel is FP16-only (Triton atomic_add has no BF16/FP8 path), directly conflicting with this team's FP8 serving. Net: a real edge/single-user decode win, not a production-vLLM-on-H100 win.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only is NOT sufficient, contrary to the 'yes-pure-substrate' claim. What the substrate would actually have to build/do, none of which is covered by GOT-patching cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM entry points: (a) Per-call, on the LIVE input activation vector, compute a magnitude mask against the offline per-tensor threshold (a new pre-GEMM reduction kernel) — the substrate can read the activation pointer it intercepts, so this part is reachable. (b) SUBSTITUTE the dense cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM with TEAL's specialized Triton sparse-GEMV (DejaVu-derived: column-major weight storage, selective column loading by mask, SplitK). This requires the weights to be pre-reordered to column-major and the dense call structurally replaced — not a transparent shim over cuBLAS, and the official repo states plainly it 'cannot be done purely through GEMM interception' and needs model-forward-pass changes. (c) There is NO vLLM integration in the TEAL repo (it runs on gpt-fast/HF standalone, authors call it a 'proof of concept'); delivering it under unmodified vLLM means the substrate must replicate the sparsification hooks vLLM never exposes. (d) FP16-only kernel vs the team's FP8 serving — a new FP8 sparse-GEMV would have to be written from scratch. So realistically this is needs-model-or-framework-grade engineering (custom kernel + weight relayout + per-call mask kernel), and even fully built it only helps at batch-1 — which production vLLM does not run. The substrate CAN do the interception plumbing; it cannot make a batch-collapsing, FP16-only technique pay off in FP8 batched serving.
assessment.reasoning: Primary source (arXiv 2408.14690 v3 HTML): headline 1.53x/1.8x is A6000 single-batch at 40%/50%; A100 is 1.25-1.34x / 1.33-1.45x; baseline is torch.compile/gpt-fast with CUDA graphs; PPL Llama-2-7B 5.07->5.22 (40%) ->5.43 (50%), Mistral-7B 4.92->5.13->5.31; speedup explicitly targets memory-bandwidth-bound single-batch decode; thresholds calibrated offline from C4. The paper itself states 'TEAL exhibits substantial sparsity in the low-batch setting but does not scale as well to higher batch sizes, which is a limitation of most activation sparsity work,' and shows W_down sparsity ~60%->~38% at batch=4. Official repo (github.com/FasterDecoding/TEAL): custom Triton sparse-GEMV + forward-pass modification required, 'cannot be done purely through GEMM interception,' no vLLM integration, gpt-fast baseline, FP16 only (BF16 unsupported, Triton atomic_add), described as proof-of-concept. Critique/follow-up (Polar Sparsity, arXiv 2505.14884, NeurIPS 2025, A100): documents union-sparsity-vanishes-with-batch directly, says conventional MLP activation sparsity 'breaks down under batched workloads,' which is why Polar pivots to attention-head sparsity (batch-invariant) and itself requires TRAINED routers — confirming the batched-serving path is not training-free. This matches the team's own prior finding that contextual/activation sparsity fails on SwiGLU under realistic load; TEAL fixes the SwiGLU fidelity issue (sparsifies all hidden states) but not the batching-collapse issue, which is the one that matters for vLLM-on-H100.
