assessment.technique: CATS (Contextually-Aware Thresholding for Sparsity) — arXiv 2404.08763, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab
assessment.honest_gain: For this team's setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8, BATCHED/SATURATED serving): expected gain ~0%, plausibly negative. The headline 18% (Llama-2-7B) / 21% (Mistral-7B) end-to-end throughput and ~15% wall-clock latency are a SINGLE CONFIG: batch size 1, beam width 1, L40S GPU, FP32 (paper's own words: 'We test the generation throughput at batch size 1 and beam width 1'). The mechanism is reduced WEIGHT MEMORY LOADS in the MLP — it works ONLY because batch-1 decode is memory-bound (paper: 'MLP blocks are known to be memory-bound during inference... latency can be reduced if memory access is reduced'). Under batched serving the benefit collapses via UNION sparsity (a neuron is retained if active for ANY sequence in the batch): Polar Sparsity (NeurIPS 2025) measures union activation rising from ~10% at batch 1 to ~30-40% by batch 64 and states 'MLP sparsity is less effective at scale'; TEAL (ICLR 2025) independently confirms 'does not scale well to higher batch sizes... a limitation of most activation sparsity work.' At scale the gather kernel becomes a compute-bound loser vs dense BMM. FP8 (which this team already runs) further halves the weight-stream the whole memory-bound benefit rests on, shrinking absorbable headroom. Net: pay 1.04% (Mistral) / 1.56% (Llama-2) zero-shot accuracy at 50% for a speedup that exists only in the batch-1 corner the team does not serve. Realistic deployed gain at production batch sizes: negligible.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-only does NOT suffice — the research pass's 'yes-pure-substrate' claim is wrong. The CATS sparse kernel is explicitly NOT a drop-in cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM swap (paper Appendix D / Algorithm 1): it needs the live SiLU gate activations plus a calibrated threshold passed in at runtime, computes a per-token binary mask (Mask=1 if |gate|>=t), and fuses a gather/scatter over W_up columns and W_down rows. To deliver this the substrate would have to (1) semantically recognize the gate->up->down SwiGLU MLP triple across separate intercepted GEMM calls, (2) capture the intermediate gate activation tensor between those calls, (3) replace the up/down GEMMs with a custom fused gather-GEMV keyed on that mask. That is a structural rewrite of the model's MLP forward, not a call-level GEMM substitution at the cuBLAS GOT boundary. The masking/gather lives INSIDE the model forward, which intercept-only cannot author. vLLM has no native dynamic-activation-sparsity path (open issue vllm-project/vllm#10259); delivering CATS requires model-cooperation or a vLLM custom layer/kernel — both excluded by the substrate definition. Even if hosted, the gain still evaporates at production batch (above).
assessment.reasoning: Primary source: CATS paper (arXiv 2404.08763v1, Stanford). Verified setup via WebFetch: batch=1, beam=1, L40S, FP32; throughput 18% (Llama-2-7B) / 21% (Mistral-7B) at 50%; MLP block ~40%@50% / ~70%@70%; accuracy 68.90 vs 69.94 (Mistral, -1.04%) and 64.33 vs 65.89 (Llama-2, -1.56%) zero-shot. Kernel mechanism (memory-load reduction, runtime mask, fused gather, NOT a GEMM drop-in) confirmed from the same paper's Algorithm 1 / Appendix D. Batch-collapse corroborated by THREE independent follow-ups: (a) Polar Sparsity, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv 2505.14884) — 'union neuron sparsity in MLP layers decreases rapidly with batch size, illustrating why MLP sparsity is less effective at scale'; union ~10%@b1 -> ~30-40%@b64; MLP sparsity helps only small-batch low-latency while head sparsity is the batched lever; gather-based sparse execution caps below dense BMM in the compute-bound region. (b) TEAL, ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2408.14690) — 'does not scale well to higher batch sizes, which is a limitation of most activation sparsity work.' (c) vLLM issue #10259 confirms no native support; community notes gather-based sparse execution is a fundamental compute-bound limitation at scale. This also matches the team's own established finding that contextual/activation sparsity fails on SwiGLU at the fidelity level — CATS only 'wins' at batch-1 via a memory-load mechanism the team already characterized as a batch-1-only lever. Sources: arxiv.org/abs/2404.08763, scalingintelligence.stanford.edu/pubs/CATSpaper, arxiv.org/abs/2505.14884, arxiv.org/abs/2408.14690, github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/10259.

technique.name: PowerInfer / DejaVu contextual sparsity (ReLU-era) — confirmed NOT applicable to SwiGLU
technique.mechanism: Predicts which MLP neurons / attention heads are active per token with a small MLP predictor, computes only the 'hot' fraction, and (PowerInfer) keeps hot neurons GPU-resident while streaming cold ones from CPU. Relies on the >90% natural activation sparsity of ReLU/ReGLU models.
technique.reported_gain: PowerInfer: up to ~11x on consumer GPU for ReLU models (ReluLLaMA); DejaVu ~2x on OPT. BUT on SiLU/SwiGLU models natural sparsity is only ~50%, and substituting ReGLU only reaches ~70% — too low to amortize predictor + gather overhead, so the speedup largely evaporates. This confirms the team's prior finding that contextual sparsity is a ReLU-era win (PowerInfer arXiv 2312.12456; Turbo Sparse arXiv 2406.05955).
technique.axis: MBU (would-be), but net gain ~0 on modern SwiGLU at serving
technique.model_dependency: needs a ReLU/ReGLU checkpoint (ReLUfication) AND trained per-layer predictors; neither exists for stock SwiGLU and both require training. A substrate cannot manufacture the sparsity that the SwiGLU activation does not have.
technique.impl_cost: N/A for substrate (blocked: requires retrained model + predictors)

assessment.technique: PowerInfer / DejaVu contextual (activation) sparsity — neuron/head predictors + hot-neuron residency, exploiting >90% natural sparsity of ReLU/ReGLU MLPs; extended by Turbo Sparse (dReLU) and Polar Sparsity (batched)
assessment.honest_gain: For H100 / 7B dense SwiGLU / vLLM / FP8 batched serving: ~0x (no realizable gain) for the MLP contextual-sparsity mechanism the technique is built on. The headline numbers are all off-setup: PowerInfer up to 11.69x is RTX-4090 single-GPU CPU-offload vs llama.cpp on a ReLU model (ReluLLaMA), batch-1, memory-bound consumer regime — explicitly NOT for A100/H100 datacenter serving (the paper states it is mostly for single-GPU local/low-batch and is slower than holding the full model on adequate GPUs). DejaVu ~2x is OPT-175B (ReLU-era). Turbo Sparse 2-5x decoding speedup is batch-1 on CPU (2.08-2.81x vs llama.cpp) / consumer hybrid GPU-CPU (2.52-4.64x, RTX 4090/2080Ti) / mobile (22.2x Mixtral on OnePlus-12 via PowerInfer-2) — never H100-batched. Critically, on stock SwiGLU the natural sparsity is only ~40% (Llama-2-7B, Turbo Sparse Table 1); substituting ReGLU reaches just 67-71%; only dReLU hits ~90%, and that requires 150B-token continued pretraining + trained per-FFN predictors. Under PRODUCTION batched serving the union of active neurons approaches dense, so MLP contextual-sparsity speedup vanishes with batch size (Polar Sparsity, NeurIPS 2025). The only batch-surviving residue is ATTENTION-HEAD sparsity (batch-invariant): Polar reports up to 2.2x e2e on OPT-66B (batch 64, A100) and ~1.85x on LLaMA-2-7B — but that path needs trained per-layer routers + a custom Selective-FlashAttention kernel, and is reported on bf16/A100, not FP8/H100/vLLM, with no FP8 number to cite. Honest expected gain for THIS team via intercept-only substrate on stock SwiGLU: zero.
assessment.substrate_reality: A CUDA-interposition substrate (GOT-patch cuBLAS/cutlass GEMM, intercept kernels, classifier, clocks, runs under unmodified vLLM, no retrain, no vLLM fork) CANNOT deliver this technique. Three hard blockers, each independently fatal: (1) The substrate cannot manufacture sparsity that the SwiGLU activation does not produce — at ~40% natural sparsity (and union->dense under batching) there is nothing to gate. (2) The technique's sparsity REQUIRES model surgery the substrate cannot perform: ReLUfication/dReLU is continued pretraining (150B tokens) producing a new checkpoint, plus trained per-layer/per-FFN predictor (or router) networks that are additional learned weights. Intercept-only injection cannot create trained predictors. (3) Even the one batch-robust path (Polar attention-head sparsity) needs (a) trained routers AND (b) a custom Selective-FlashAttention GPU kernel that vLLM's attention path must actually call — i.e., model weights + a framework/kernel change, not transparent GEMM interception. vLLM's attention is FlashAttention (not cuBLAS), so even the interception surface is wrong. Conclusion: this is needs-model-training + framework-change, with no intercept-only variant. The substrate could at most host pre-trained routers if a cooperating model shipped them — outside the stated no-retrain constraint. Recommend SHELVE; do not build. (This corroborates the team's prior 'contextual sparsity FAILS on SwiGLU' finding and adds the production-batching reason: union->dense, not just low per-token sparsity.)
assessment.reasoning: Sources: PowerInfer (arXiv 2312.12456, SOSP'24) — up to 11.69x vs llama.cpp on RTX 4090, exploits ~80% inactivation in OPT-30B (ReLU), explicitly local/single-GPU/low-batch, slower than full-GPU residency; reaches 82% of A100 token-rate on a consumer GPU — i.e., a consumer-substitution win, not a datacenter win (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12456, https://ipads.se.sjtu.edu.cn/_media/publications/song-sosp24.pdf). Turbo Sparse / dReLU (arXiv 2406.05955) — SwiGLU Llama-2-7B sparsity 40%, ReGLU 67-71%, dReLU ~90% but via 150B-token continued pretraining + per-FFN predictor module trained in SFT; speedups 2.08-2.81x CPU / 2.52-4.64x consumer hybrid GPU-CPU / 22.2x mobile Mixtral on PowerInfer-2 — all batch-1, none H100-batched (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05955v2, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05955). DejaVu — ~2x on OPT-175B, ReLU-era contextual sparsity with trained predictors. Polar Sparsity (arXiv 2505.14884, NeurIPS 2025) is the decisive production critique: 'contextual sparsity does not scale to large batch sizes due to union of active neurons quickly approaching dense computation'; MLP sparsity vanishes under batching while attention-head sparsity stays batch-invariant; for non-ReLU (LLaMA/Mistral) they apply ONLY attention-head sparsity because MLP sparsification is ineffective; up to 2.2x e2e (OPT-66B batch 64) / 1.85x LLaMA-2-7B on A100, requiring trained per-layer routers + custom Selective-FlashAttention kernel (https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14884, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14884). The corpus also confirms the general SwiGLU verdict: 'modern LLMs using SwiGLU do not exhibit natural sparsity' and 'as MLP layers become more compute-efficient under batching, their sparsity vanishes' (training-free activation sparsity / TEAL line, arXiv 2408.14690 — TEAL only ~1.8x and at low batch). Net: the originally-claimed deliverability ('no-needs-model-training') is wrong on inspection — every variant needs either a ReLUfied/dReLU checkpoint or trained predictors/routers (and the batch-robust path also needs a custom kernel), so it is firmly needs-model-training/framework-change, and the gains do not survive H100 batched FP8 serving.

technique.name: ProSparse / ReLUfication (activation-sparsity recovery via fine-tuning)
technique.mechanism: Replaces SiLU/SwiGLU with ReLU and applies progressive sparsity regularization + fine-tuning to push activation sparsity to ~89% while preserving accuracy, restoring the ReLU-era contextual-sparsity regime so PowerInfer-style serving works.
technique.reported_gain: 89.32% sparsity on Llama-2-7B, 88.80% on Llama-2-13B with accuracy comparable to the Swish original; up to 4.52x inference speedup (custom sparse kernels) / 4.65x with PowerInfer (ProSparse, arXiv 2402.13516, COLING 2025).
technique.model_dependency: needs full ReLUfication + sparsity-regularized fine-tuning to produce a new checkpoint (SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b on HF). Out of bounds for a no-retraining substrate — but note: if the customer ships a ProSparse checkpoint, the substrate could then host the sparse-GEMV serving kernel (yes-with-model-cooperation in that narrow case).
technique.impl_cost: N/A for substrate as a no-retrain product (model training is the blocker)

assessment.technique: ProSparse / ReLUfication (activation-sparsity recovery via sparsity-regularized fine-tuning), arXiv 2402.13516 (COLING 2025), with PowerInfer-style sparse-FFN serving.
assessment.honest_gain: For THIS team's setup (H100, 7B dense, unmodified vLLM, batched/saturated FP8 serving): ~1.0x. Effectively no win. The headline 4.52x (custom sparse kernels) / 4.65x (PowerInfer vs llama.cpp) is a SINGLE-REQUEST, GPU-CPU-OFFLOAD, CONSUMER-GPU number — exactly the batch-1 regime where the union of active neurons across a batch is still small. It does NOT transfer to a saturated vLLM server. Confirmation chain: (a) PowerInfer's own measurements say for batch sizes under ~32 the offload helps because few neurons are hot; the Q-Infer follow-up (DL.ACM 3764589) reports PowerInfer is ~2x SLOWER than dense at large batch. (b) The fraction of highly-activated neurons rises from <1% at batch=1 to ~75% at batch=32 — the union approaches dense compute, so the sparse-FFN kernel reverts to a dense GEMM with overhead. (c) Polar Sparsity (NeurIPS 2025, A100) explicitly tested ProSparse/Sparse-LLaMA and found MLP sparsity has "high variance and degrading trends at larger batch sizes," so they ABANDONED MLP/FFN sparsity for LLaMA-class models entirely and kept only attention-head sparsity — net system speedup up to 2.2x across models, ~1.85x for Llama-2-7B, and only at large batch (modest at batch=1). Honest ceiling if the team adopted the BATCH-ROBUST successor (Polar attention-head sparsity, not ProSparse-FFN): maybe 1.3-1.85x throughput on attention-bound regimes, but that still needs sparse-aware kernels vLLM does not ship and is orthogonal to FFN ReLUfication. ProSparse FFN sparsity itself: ~1.0x in production serving.
assessment.substrate_reality: Two walls, either fatal. WALL 1 (model retrain): ProSparse REQUIRES a new checkpoint (full ReLUfication + progressive sparsity-regularized fine-tuning; SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b on HF is a distinct model, not Mistral/Llama you serve). A CUDA-interposition substrate that does not retrain and does not fork vLLM cannot produce this — out of bounds by definition. The 'no-needs-model-training' deliverability tag in the research pass is simply wrong for the headline gain. WALL 2 (the narrow 'customer ships a ProSparse checkpoint' case still fails in production): even granting the checkpoint, what the substrate would host is a sparse-GEMV/sparse-FFN kernel that conditionally skips cold neurons per-token. To deliver a win it must (i) intercept the gate/up/down GEMMs, (ii) run an activation predictor, (iii) gather only hot neuron rows, (iv) dispatch a sparse kernel — but in vLLM's continuous-batching saturated regime the per-token hot sets UNION across the batch and the gathered weight set approaches the full weight matrix, so the sparse kernel reverts to dense + gather overhead and can be slower than the cutlass dense GEMM the team already measured as the floor. Intercept-only is NOT enough: this needs a predictor model co-located with the checkpoint and a scatter/gather memory layout, i.e., model+framework cooperation, and it only pays off at batch~1 (which the team does not run saturated). Note this also directly re-confirms the team's own established constraint that contextual/activation sparsity fails on SwiGLU at batch scale — ProSparse only 'fixes' it by swapping in a different model, which the substrate cannot do.
assessment.reasoning: Sources: ProSparse paper arXiv 2402.13516 v7 / aclanthology 2025.coling-main.180 — 89.32% sparsity Llama-2-7B, 88.80% Llama-2-13B, accuracy comparable to Swish (ProSparse-7B avg 38.46% vs 37.96%; ProSparse-13B 44.90% vs 44.06% — accuracy claim holds, it is genuinely near-lossless), up to 4.52x PowerInfer-vs-llama.cpp and sparse-GPU-operator speedups 2.44x/1.70x; paper does NOT specify datacenter hardware and the tok/s framing is single-sequence (batch-1). The HF model card (SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b) confirms it is a fine-tuned checkpoint requiring training. CRITICAL CRITIQUE — Polar Sparsity (arXiv 2505.14884, NeurIPS 2025, run on NVIDIA DGX A100 80GB): 'contextual sparsity does not scale to large batch sizes due to union of active neurons quickly approaching dense computation'; Figure 8(b) shows ProSparse Sparse-LLaMA MLP sparsity is high-variance and degrades with batch; they pivot to attention-head sparsity (batch-invariant) for LLaMA models, achieving up to 2.2x end-to-end (1.85x Llama-2-7B), modest at batch=1. PowerInfer (SOSP 2024, arXiv 2312.12456) is explicitly 'serving with a CONSUMER-grade GPU' via GPU-CPU offload; its win evaporates above batch~32. Q-Infer (ACM 3764589) reports PowerInfer ~2x slower than dense at large batch and the highly-activated-neuron fraction climbing <1%@batch1 to ~75%@batch32. vLLM has no production ProSparse activation-sparsity path (only the SJTU sparse_gpu_operator repo exists, standalone CUDA/CANN ops, not integrated into vLLM serving). Net: the gain is real but mis-scoped — it is a batch-1 consumer-GPU offload result, superseded for batched serving by Polar Sparsity which itself discards the FFN-sparsity mechanism this technique relies on. Not deliverable by a no-retrain, no-vLLM-fork, intercept-only substrate on H100 batched FP8 7B serving.

research.summary: There IS a defensible substrate-position product, and it is mostly about MULTI-TENANCY, POWER, and RELIABILITY — not single-stream MFU (which the team has already shown is ~68%-capped). Three findings are load-bearing. (1) Phase-aware DVFS is the strongest pure-substrate win: because decode is memory-bound and frequency-insensitive, clocking DOWN only the decode phase via NVML application clocks yields 25-42% energy savings (and ~1.4x tok/W) at <3.5% SLO violation and near-zero throughput loss — refining the team's "DVFS trades throughput" prior, since the loss only appears if you also throttle the compute-bound prefill; recent work shows clock-locking Pareto-dominates power-capping. A substrate is the natural home because it already sees the prefill/decode phase boundary across processes and owns NVML. (2) Cross-tenant GPU sharing (MuxServe 1.8x throughput / 2.9x more requests-within-SLO; Prism >2x cost / 3.3x SLO; dynamic-MIG ~32% lower SLO-miss, ~15% better p99) is real and large, but the strongest versions need a custom RUNTIME (unified KV/memory manager) — a substrate can deliver the SM-partitioning/MPS scheduling and dynamic MIG/placement portion, and CUDA-interposition fractional-GPU is already productized (Backend.AI, Bitfusion, Run:ai, TensorFusion), but true cross-model GEMM batching needs framework cooperation. (3) SDC/reliability is a genuine white space: SDC hits ~1-in-1000 devices, Meta runs FleetScanner/Ripple/Hardware-Sentinel internally, and NO vendor offers inline SDC detection as a customer-facing serving SLA — exactly the seam an inline GEMM-interception checker sits in (the team has already built and measured this at +3% detector / +51% eager-host tax). The honest caveat across all of these: the biggest single-stream efficiency levers are closed; the substrate's edge is cross-process orchestration, power, and reliability — features frameworks structurally can't provide because each vLLM/TRT-LLM process sees only itself.

techniques.name: Phase-aware DVFS (clock-down memory-bound decode, clock-up/mid-band prefill) via NVML
techniques.mechanism: Decode is memory-bound and largely frequency-insensitive, so the substrate sets a low SM clock during decode and a mid/high clock during prefill via NVML application-clock APIs, sitting outside the critical path. It exploits the prefill/decode phase boundary that a cross-process substrate can already observe.
techniques.reported_gain: GreenLLM: up to 34% total energy reduction vs NVIDIA default DVFS on Azure traces, 6.8-27.5% on Alibaba traces, <3.5% SLO violations, ~no throughput loss, on 8xA100 (arXiv 2508.16449). Phase-aware characterization: 41.9% avg energy reduction with 2.8% latency increase across 5 models, prefill 2842MHz / decode 180MHz (arXiv 2605.11999). EcoInfer: up to 25.4% avg energy savings; iteration-level DVFS 22.8-45.5% under varying SLOs. 'Clock-locking Pareto-dominates power-capping, recovering up to 32% of decode energy at minimal throughput loss.' Consistent with team's own ~1.4x tok/W.
techniques.axis: TPW (tokens/watt, energy/cost) — primarily; latency-neutral
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: days-to-weeks (NVML clock control + phase classifier; team already has DVFS at 1.4x tok/W committed)
sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.11999v1 (The Illusion of Power Capping in LLM Decode)

techniques.name: Cross-tenant SM-multiplexing of multiple LLMs (spatial-temporal, MPS/green-context SM partitioning)
techniques.mechanism: Co-locate multiple LLMs on one GPU and dynamically assign SMs at runtime (NVIDIA MPS / green-context granularity), overlapping one model's memory-bound decode with another's compute-bound prefill to fill the ~95% idle decode compute the team measured. The STRONGEST version (MuxServe/Prism) also needs a unified KV/memory manager = a custom runtime.
techniques.reported_gain: MuxServe: up to 1.8x throughput over spatial-partition/temporal-multiplex baselines, OR 2.9x more requests within 99% SLO; tested 19 LLMs (LLaMA 7B-65B) on 4-node 8xA100-80GB (arXiv 2404.02015). Prism: >2x cost savings and 3.3x SLO attainment vs SOTA, via on-demand virtual-to-physical page mapping + two-level scheduling (arXiv 2505.04021).
techniques.axis: throughput and TPW (cost-per-token via higher utilization)
techniques.model_dependency: none model-side, but needs serving-runtime cooperation for the unified KV/memory manager; substrate alone can do the MPS/SM-partition scheduling + placement, not the cross-model KV manager
techniques.impl_cost: weeks-to-months (MPS/green-context scheduler is weeks; full MuxServe-class unified memory manager is months and arguably a framework change)

techniques.name: Dynamic MIG/MPS reconfiguration + topology/PCIe-aware placement (noisy-neighbor control)
techniques.mechanism: A host-level controller (VM-deployable, fabric-agnostic) dynamically reconfigures MIG partitions, applies MPS quotas and cgroup I/O guardrails, and uses topology hints for PCIe-aware placement, gated by dwell/cool-down to avoid thrash. Cross-tenant tail sampling drives the decisions — visibility a single framework process lacks.
techniques.reported_gain: ~32% reduction in SLO miss-rate and ~15% p99 latency improvement at <=5% throughput cost vs static MIG + naive placement, on single host and 2-node 16-GPU cluster; TTFT p99 ~10-15% better at <=5% cost on vLLM serving OLMo-2-7B-Instruct (arXiv 2508.20274, 'Predictable LLM Serving on GPU Clusters'). Dynamic MIG reconfiguration is the single largest p99-reduction component.
techniques.axis: latency (p99/TTFT tails) and throughput-per-cost under multi-tenancy
techniques.model_dependency: none model-side; needs orchestrator/control-plane hooks for MIG reconfig (NVML/CUDA) and per-tenant telemetry — sits at substrate/host-controller layer, not inside vLLM
techniques.impl_cost: weeks (MIG/MPS control + placement controller; MIG reconfig is an NVML/driver op)
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20274 (Predictable LLM Serving on GPU Clusters)

techniques.name: Inline SDC / silent-fault detection as a serving reliability SLA (GEMM-interception checker)
techniques.mechanism: Intercept cuBLAS/cutlass GEMMs at the driver level and periodically re-verify outputs (recompute/ABFT/Freivalds-style) to catch silent data corruption during live serving — a per-GPU/per-tenant correctness signal frameworks don't produce. This is the team's own validated R.A path.
techniques.reported_gain: Problem prevalence: SDC affects ~1-in-1000 devices (Meta), up from ~1-in-1,000,000 for soft errors; 78% of Llama-3 pretraining interruptions were hardware. Meta uses FleetScanner (45-60 day fleet sweep), Ripple (ms-s inline), Hardware Sentinel (+41% over test-based) — all INTERNAL, none customer-facing. Team's measured cost: +3.1% with detector at N=45 / +51% eager-host tax (cuBLAS-interception requires eager), 0 false positives over ~5376 checks, persistent SDC caught within N steps, in real vLLM Mistral-7B (team memory: cipher-ra-realvllm-validation).
techniques.axis: reliability/correctness SLA (new product axis, not raw efficiency) — defensible because it is a white space
techniques.model_dependency: none (intercepts GEMMs, recomputes; no draft model, no retraining)
techniques.impl_cost: weeks (team has already built and measured it; productizing as an SLA is integration + the eager-host tax tradeoff)
sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.04213 (Anatomy of Silent Data Corruption: GPU Error Pattern Study)

techniques.name: Transparent fractional-GPU / CUDA-interposition multi-tenancy (productized substrate pattern)
techniques.mechanism: Intercept CUDA driver/runtime calls (LD_PRELOAD or driver-level) to enforce per-tenant compute/memory limits, isolate workloads, and even remote/pool GPUs across hosts — no model or framework changes. Proves the substrate position is commercially defensible.
techniques.reported_gain: No single clean academic throughput number; this is a PRODUCT category, not a paper. Evidence of viability: Backend.AI patented fractional-GPU via CUDA-API interception in-container; Bitfusion intercepts at CUDA driver level for pooling/remoting; Run:ai/TensorFusion offer fractional GPU; rCUDA (400+ citations) is the academic root. G-Safe adds safe multi-tenant isolation at the runtime/driver library level (arXiv 2401.09290). Gains are utilization/packing-driven (filling idle GPUs), not a fixed multiplier.
techniques.axis: throughput-per-cost (utilization/density) under multi-tenancy
techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: weeks-to-months (interception + isolation is the core substrate; safe memory isolation a la G-Safe is the hard part)
sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.09290v1 (G-Safe: Safe GPU Sharing in Multi-Tenant Environments)

techniques.name: Power-capping for cost in power-constrained datacenters (substrate as power broker)
techniques.mechanism: Cap per-GPU power via NVML to maximize tokens/sec/watt (or fit more GPUs under a fixed grid/rack power budget) — a fleet-level lever a per-process framework cannot coordinate. Distinct from phase-aware DVFS: this is a deliberate throughput-for-power trade when power (not silicon) is the binding constraint.
techniques.reported_gain: Datacenters are increasingly power-constrained; tokens/sec/watt is the operator metric. Team's own measure: ~1.4x tok/W lossless via DVFS, more if capping at load. Economic stakes: on a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster, 55% vs 85% utilization is -$330k vs +$340k/month.

techniques.model_dependency: none
techniques.impl_cost: days (NVML power-cap; team already has it) — value is in the fleet-coordination policy, not the mechanism

assessment.technique: Phase-aware DVFS (clock-down memory-bound decode, clock-up/mid-band prefill) via NVML application/locked clocks, from a cross-process CUDA-interposition substrate
assessment.honest_gain: This is an ENERGY / tok-per-watt lever, not a throughput or MFU lever, and the substrate can deliver only a watered-down version of the headline. Honest expectation for H100 / 7B-dense GQA (Mistral/Llama) / vLLM / FP8: a STATIC low SM clock during decode-dominated operation buys roughly 1.3-1.4x tok/W at under 1-3% throughput loss — i.e. it recovers about 25-32% of DECODE energy, NOT 34-42% of TOTAL serving energy. This is exactly consistent with the team's own measured ~1.4x tok/W DVFS result, so it adds essentially nothing new. The big headline numbers do not transfer: (a) GreenLLM's 'up to 34%' (28-34% Azure, 6.8-27.5% Alibaba, arXiv 2508.16449) is on 8xA100 under NVIDIA Dynamo with P/D execution pools, and even there it COLLAPSES to 6.8% near saturation as clocks rise to protect SLOs; (b) the 41.9-42% / 2842->180MHz figure (arXiv 2501.08219) is OFFLINE replay, batch 1/4/8, on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (not H100), and the authors EXPLICITLY disclaim continuous batching, chunked prefill, and production serving ('empirical observations rather than deployment prescriptions'); (c) the 'clock-locking Pareto-dominates power-capping, up to 32% of decode energy at <1% throughput loss' claim (arXiv 2605.11999) is single-card H200, ISOLATED decode phase, ~4B GQA/MLA/Mamba models, BS=1-32 — and even it warns that at BS=32 with long context (>=16K) the workload turns compute-bound and savings fall to 5-15% with the optimal clock rising. Net for this team: a real but small, throughput-trading energy win, biggest at low/medium load, shrinking toward zero exactly where a neocloud runs (batched, saturated). Caution: NVML application clocks are deprecated and slated for removal in CUDA 14.0; must migrate to nvmlDeviceSetGpuLockedClocks.
assessment.substrate_reality: Intercept-ONLY is NOT sufficient for the per-iteration, phase-aware version that produces the best published numbers; the substrate can only deliver a coarse static/feedback variant. Three hard walls: (1) PHASE BOUNDARY IS NOT CLEANLY OBSERVABLE under default vLLM. vLLM's chunked prefill INTENTIONALLY mixes prefill and decode tokens in the same scheduler iteration to raise utilization, so there is no clean prefill->decode boundary for a cross-process substrate to clock against. The cleanest published systems sidestep this only via prefill/decode DISAGGREGATION (separate GPU instances) — VoltanaLLM (arXiv 2509.04827) and BiScale/DualScale (arXiv 2602.18755) both require P/D disaggregation, and VoltanaLLM is implemented INSIDE SGLang (EcoFreq/EcoRoute/EcoPred), not under an unmodified framework. (2) SWITCHING LATENCY kills per-iteration control from outside the framework. Measured SM-clock switch latency (arXiv 2502.20075) is ~22.7ms worst-case on A100 and ~477ms on GH200; a 7B decode iteration is single-digit ms, so per-token NVML switching is infeasible. CUDA also gives NO forward-progress/concurrency guarantee across green-context partitions. Intercept-only therefore buys the substrate a multi-tenant PLACEMENT/admission-control product (real and useful for a fleet: which models share which GPU, MPS quota enforcement, noisy-neighbor guarding) but NOT the throughput multiplier, which needs framework cooperation (model executor + KV manager changes) the charter forbids.

Honest cost for THIS setup (H100, 7B dense, vLLM, FP8): the team's own measured +3.1% detector cost at N=45 is realistic ONLY in eager mode, and the dominant real cost is the +51% eager-host tax (2.05x) because cuBLAS GOT-interception forces enforce_eager and forfeits CUDA-graph decode (team memory cipher-ra-realvllm-validation: eager 629 tok/s vs cudagraph 1289). So the honest production cost is ~52% throughput vs a cudagraph FP8 vLLM baseline, not 3%. The detection capability itself is real and literature-endorsed: persistent SDC caught within N steps, 0 false positives over ~5376 checks at T=0 bit-exact. But the VALUE side is unquantified — no public source measures SDC's actual inference-output error rate, and no cloud sells a correctness SLA, so willingness-to-pay is unproven. Prevalence framing checks out (~1-in-1000 devices, Meta/Google/Alibaba) but the team's cited "78% Llama-3 hardware interruptions" is wrong: Meta's 2025 blog says >66% (and the 78% figure is not the one Meta published).

(2) Coverage is linear-GEMM-only; FlashAttention is not cuBLAS (>99% of decode FLOPs are linears for short ctx, but attention and all non-linear ops are a NAMED BLIND SPOT — and ABFT provably cannot cover non-linear ops). (3) The detector's recompute is SAME-GPU, so it only catches faults that reproduce deterministically on recompute; the mercurial-core / data-dependent CEE class (Google HotOS'21, Meta) is often non-deterministic w.r.t. voltage/temp/aging and same-GPU recompute is BLIND to it — that genuinely needs DMR / a second GPU / shadow replica (a framework/orchestration change). (4) FP8 serving narrows the margin: SDC magnitudes can be within FP8/float error bounds, which is exactly why the 2025 ACL paper found ABFT/checksum "fails to reliably detect SDCs with high precision and recall." The team's choice of T=0 bit-exact full-recompute (not ABFT checksum) sidesteps that precision/recall failure — so the substrate's actual shipped mechanism is the literature-RECOMMENDED one ("additional recomputation may be the best solution"), which is a point in its favor.

The throughput/MFU moat for an intercept-only substrate on H100/7B-dense/vLLM is **small and mostly already captured by modern vLLM.** Every large decode win in the dossier (EAGLE-class spec-decode, megakernels, W4A16) either (a) lives in the serving runtime above the GEMM boundary, (b) needs a model-side artifact (trained head / pre-quantized checkpoint), or (c) goes break-even-to-negative in this team's saturated-batch operating point. The one pure-substrate precision lever (FP8) the team already measured at ~1.05–1.24x.

**So the defensible product is NOT a throughput hero. It is a cross-tenant efficiency-and-reliability orchestrator that the interposition position uniquely enables — with FP8/kernel-dispatch as the in-band efficiency floor and the team's already-built SDC/per-GPU-reliability detection (R.A/R.C) as the real differentiated value.** Below I give both: the small-but-real efficiency product, and the actually-defensible moat.

---

## 1. THE PRODUCT

**"CIPHER Fleet Guard + Efficiency Floor"** — a CUDA-interposition control plane that runs UNDER unmodified vLLM and delivers two things no vLLM feature delivers from that position:

- **(A) In-band correctness + per-GPU reliability detection** across processes/tenants (SDC/silent-corruption catch, per-GPU degraded-GPU verdict, 0-FP) — the team has already BUILT and validated this inside real vLLM (R.A: detector fires, catches injected SDC, 0 FP, ~3% detector cost eager; R.C: per-GPU DEGRADED verdict, 0-FP over 4352+ checks).
- **(B) An efficiency floor it can actually actuate from the driver seam:** FP8 weight-side precision (pure-substrate, proven), kernel-library dispatch (FA3/FlashInfer behind intercepted calls), and cross-tenant DVFS/clock/power orchestration (~1.4x tok/W lossless, only deployable as a fleet-level scheduler decision — which is exactly the substrate's cross-process vantage).

**Expected composed gain (honest):** the efficiency floor is **~1.1–1.3x throughput in batched serving / ~1.5x MBU at batch-1 / ~1.4x tok/W under power headroom (NOT at full load), all already roughly at the team's measured ceiling.** The *product value* is not that multiplier — it is that the substrate adds **silent-data-corruption + degraded-GPU detection at <~3% cost with 0 false positives, cross-tenant, with zero model retrain and zero vLLM fork.** That is the differentiated, defensible deliverable.

**Why the substrate position is the right vehicle:** correctness/reliability detection and cross-tenant power/clock orchestration genuinely require seeing GEMM/kernel calls across process boundaries and setting GPU state — capabilities that live precisely at the driver-interposition layer and NOT in any single vLLM process. Every throughput technique, by contrast, lives above the GEMM boundary, so the substrate has no structural advantage there.

## 2. THE TECHNIQUE STACK

Only techniques the assessments rated real-and-deliverable or real-but-needs-model-or-framework:

| # | Technique | Honest gain | Axis | Model dependency | Substrate fit |
|---|-----------|-------------|------|------------------|---------------|
| 1 | **FP8 (E4M3) weight-side precision** | ~1.5x MBU @batch-1; ~1.1–1.3x throughput batched; ~0.5–2pp accuracy (task-dependent; math/long-ctx worst) | MBU/throughput | **none** for weight-side cast (clean part = effectively W8A16; full W8A8 needs fused activation-cast cooperation to stay cheap) | real-but-needs-framework for *fused* W8A8; pure-substrate for weight-side |
| 2 | **Kernel-library dispatch (FA3 / Flash-Decoding / FlashInfer)** | FA3 prefill MFU ~75% of peak vs FA2 ~35%; Flash-Decoding up to 8x long-ctx batch-1; FlashInfer 29–69% ITL — but **marginal over an up-to-date vLLM that already calls these** | MFU (prefill) / long-ctx decode latency | **none** | yes-pure-substrate (but small delta vs current vLLM) |
| 3 | **Cross-tenant DVFS / clock-power orchestration** | ~1.4x tok/W lossless (trades throughput; not deployable at full load) | TPW | none | substrate-unique (needs cross-process vantage + GPU state setting) |
| 4 | **(Optional, model-cooperation) AWQ/GPTQ W4A16 + Marlin** | ~1.5–2x **latency** at batch-1/low-QPS; **throughput-neutral-to-negative** under saturation on VRAM-abundant H100; ~0.05–0.2 PPL | MBU (memory-bound decode only) | **needs pre-quantized checkpoint** (calibration + Marlin repack) | needs-model-cooperation; substrate only *hosts* the kernel, which vLLM already does given the checkpoint |

**Compose:** FP8 weight-side (1) + kernel dispatch (2) form the in-band efficiency floor; DVFS (3) is the cross-tenant TPW lever; W4A16 (4) is an OPT-IN latency mode for interactive/low-QPS tenants only, and only if a quantized checkpoint is supplied — it is NOT a substrate-native win.

**Explicitly model-dependent:** #4 needs a quantized checkpoint. #1's *cheap fused* form needs framework cooperation. EAGLE-3 (best spec-decode) was rated real-but-needs-model-or-framework but is **excluded from the shippable stack** because it requires BOTH a trained per-model head AND vLLM runtime tree-verification — the substrate can deliver neither, and the gain is ~break-even/negative in the team's saturated regime.

## 3. SUBSTRATE-UNIQUE MOAT

What only the interposition position can do (so this is not "just use vLLM features"):

1. **Cross-process / cross-tenant SDC + degraded-GPU detection at the GEMM seam.** vLLM sees one process; the substrate GOT-patches cuBLAS across every tenant on the GPU and can re-run/checksum GEMM outputs to catch silent corruption and localize a degraded GPU — already proven (R.A: 0-FP, catches injected bit-flips inside real vLLM; R.C: per-GPU DEGRADED verdict, descriptor = SDC-pid == NVML-pid == cohort-tgid). No vLLM feature does this; DCGM/NVML catch hardware counters, not correctness.
2. **Fleet-level DVFS/power arbitration informed by what's actually running.** The substrate classifies the live workload across processes and sets clocks/power — a decision no single vLLM process can make because it can't see its co-tenants.
3. **Zero-touch deployment.** Runs under unmodified vLLM, no retrain, no fork — the reliability layer ships without touching the customer's model or serving stack.

The moat is **safety + cross-tenant efficiency orchestration**, NOT raw tokens/sec. Be explicit about this with stakeholders.

## 4. THE HONEST CEILING

- **Best-case composed efficiency:** ~1.5x MBU at batch-1 (FP8) and ~1.4x tok/W under power headroom — i.e., roughly the team's already-measured numbers. Batched-serving throughput lift is ~1.1–1.3x and **shrinks toward 1.0x at saturation** (the team's own ~68% MFU / compute-bound regime). Kernel-dispatch delta over current vLLM is single-digit.
- **vs the frontier:** the 2–5x headline decode wins (EAGLE-3, SuffixDecoding, megakernels, W4A16-at-batch-1) are real but live in the runtime/checkpoint, so the substrate cannot capture them without becoming a serving runtime or shipping a model artifact. CIPHER does NOT close that gap.
- **What it does NOT do:** does not beat an up-to-date vLLM on tokens/sec; does not deliver speculative decoding; does not deliver FP4 (Blackwell-only — zero win on Hopper); does not turn the ~290x spare decode FLOPs into tokens (that requires spec-decode, which is framework-owned). The "more tokens per weight-stream" headroom stays unclaimed by the substrate.

3. **Cross-tenant DVFS:** Show the fleet-vantage power arbitration delivers ~1.4x tok/W on a power-headroom node and **correctly declines to actuate at full load** (honest gating).

Deliverable: one table — catch/FP/cost for reliability, and floor multipliers vs real baseline — that either supports "ship the safety+floor product" or kills it.

## 6. KILL CRITERIA

The product is NOT real if any of these measure true:

1. **Reliability cost wall:** the SDC/per-GPU detector cannot run under <~5% tok/s in the **cudagraph-on** hosting path (i.e., the +51% eager tax is unavoidable AND cudagraph-frame detection can't be made cheap). R.A already flagged in-graph injection as a measured wall (vLLM rejects external graph mutation) — if the only viable host is eager, the production reliability product dies on cost. **This is the single highest-risk kill criterion.**
2. **False positives under concurrency:** any false-positive SDC/degraded verdict across co-resident tenants at production check rates (R.C's 0-FP must hold multi-tenant, not just single-process).
3. **Efficiency floor is negative vs real baseline:** if FP8 weight-side + kernel dispatch does NOT beat the customer's current up-to-date vLLM (because vLLM already does FP8 + FlashInfer), the efficiency floor adds nothing and only the reliability story remains — and if reliability also fails (1) or (2), there is no product.
4. **No cross-tenant demand:** if real deployments are single-tenant-per-GPU, the substrate's cross-process moat evaporates and customers should just use vLLM's native FP8/kernels — the substrate is then redundant.

---

**Bottom line for the team (the honest answer you asked for):** the throughput moat is small and largely already in vLLM. The real, defensible CIPHER product is **reliability + cross-tenant efficiency orchestration** — silent-corruption/degraded-GPU detection and fleet power/clock arbitration from the driver seam — wrapped around a modest, already-proven FP8/kernel efficiency floor. Lead with safety and cross-tenant TPW, not tokens/sec. The make-or-break measurement is whether the SDC/per-GPU detector can run cheaply in the **cudagraph-on** path; everything else is already de-risked by the team's own R.A/R.C work.
